speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 106(8) I have the honour to table, in both official languages, the government's response to four petitions.
[Editor's Note: See today's Votes and Proceedings]

Mr. Speaker, I would like to bring to the attention of this House a significant occasion in housing around the world. Today is World Habitat Day and it gives us the opportunity to focus our thoughts on just how vital the home is to each and every one of us.
For most of us Canadians, it is a day to be thankful for our good fortune, for by and large we are among the best housed people in the world.

Unfortunately, many do not share our good fortune. One billion people in the world do not have decent, safe, sanitary housing. That is why the United Nations General Assembly in 1985 designated the first Monday in October as World Habitat Day.

The United Nations Centre for Human Settlements, or Habitat, has developed an ambitious plan to address shelter issues, the Global Strategy for Shelter to the Year 2000. It was adopted by the United Nations General
Assembly in December 1988. The UN believes that no country can claim to have solved all of its shelter problems and therefore all countries should make a commitment to meet shelter needs.
The theme for World Habitat Day 1989 is "Shelter, Health and the Family". This highlights the link between these critical aspects of human welfare. Without proper shelter, including housing, clean water, sanitation and community services, the risk of disease is vastly increased and a stable family life becomes almost impossible.
As one of the world's best housed nations, Canada has experience in solving housing problems that we would like to share with developing countries and with developed countries alike. On the other hand, we have not yet solved all of our own housing problems and we too can learn from the experience of other countries. Canada supports the global strategy and regularly exchanges information with the UN on Canadian initiatives to address housing issues.
Since hosting the International Habitat Conference in 1976, the federal government has provided financial contributions to the information activities of the United Nations Centre for Human Settlements.

The Habitat Information Office for North America and the Caribbean was originally located at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver and later moved to York University in Toronto. We are pleased now to house it in its new quarters in Ottawa. I am happy to announce that Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation has renewed the funding for the Information Office's activities by granting it $750,000 over three years.
I would like to close by borrowing a few words from the World Habitat Day message of the Secretary General of the United Nations. The home and family are the nucleus of the global community. The home is where we bring up our children, where we find our values, where we develop our abilities. The home is where the fabric of society is woven. In Canada, we share these principles and we continue to do all that we can here at home and

Routine Proceedings
internationally to ensure that people have adequate shelter.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Official Opposition, I am pleased to have this opportunity to draw attention to World Habitat Day. This occasion, the first Monday of October, was so designated by the United Nations General Assembly in 1985 as a means to focus the world's attention on the desperate battle to improve the shelters of hundreds of millions of people on this earth.
It is indeed shocking that a billion people around the world are in need of adequate housing, with facilities most of us here take for granted, such as clean drinking water, sanitation facilities and a safe environment for our children with educational and employment opportunities on our doorsteps.
Inadequate housing denies people the opportunity to lead fully productive lives and to help in the building of their communities. For many people throughout the world, our own country included, the lack of housing is a denial of life itself.
As the minister stated, the theme of World Habitat Day 1989 is "Shelter, Health and the Family". The theme recognizes the fact that shelter is a basic need to us all. In the absence of adequate secure shelter, there is anxiety, anger and frustration. One cannot dispute the linkage between adequate housing and good health. In the absence of adequate shelter and good health, how is the family to survive? How are parents expected to build a better future for their children when their thoughts are dominated by fears of losing what shelter, however inadequate, they possess?
The problems and heartbreak associated with inadequate housing are not limited to the squalid slums of the Third World. Here in Canada, hundreds of thousands of families and individuals live in inadequate housing, often at prices that force them to go without other necessities. The growing network of food banks and other emergency services in Canada can be directly linked to the shortage of affordable housing in this country.
This government has exacerbated the seriousness of the situation by its refusal to provide strong leadership and commit the necessary financial resources to substantially improve the living accommodations of the homeless. I might add that in this morning's The Toronto Star, the minister's statement that we do not need housing and that it is not a national issue in this country is totally irresponsible.
For those whose housing tenure is so insecure that they are in fact homeless and for parents whose children are denied the many joys which should accompany childhood, the task is great both here in Canada and around the world.
I urge the government to give this matter the attention it deserves. I applaud the initiative of the United Nations in pursuing a global strategy as a means of finding solutions to housing problems around the world. I am proud that Canadians have the opportunity to participate in this quest.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome World Habitat Day on behalf of the New Democratic Party. We hope that the location of the Habitat information office in Ottawa will result in work which will improve our efforts to house people in decent conditions both in Canada and throughout the world.
Many of us have been shocked at recent media reports of death squads in Brazil preying on the more than one million youngsters who are forced to sleep in the open each night. Another media report, most recently in The Vancouver Sun alludes to the hypocrisy of the Canadian government in its dealings with the issue of asbestos.
The United States plans to ban the use and the importation of asbestos by 1997. There is no safe level of asbestos exposure, according to health experts. The Conservative government angrily disagrees. The hypocrisy of the Canadian government in supporting a dangerous industry that is worth $300 million a year and some 2,600 jobs extends far beyond the U.S. border.
Canada's asbestos industry has busily built up export trade in the Third World, where less sophisticated societies are not so scrupulous about safety. Countries such as Pakistan, Korea and Thailand use asbestos to provide housing for the poor. This is the kind of contradiction in which the Conservative government is embroiled.

It is significant that the United Nations, which has declared this to be World Habitat Day, has found that one billion people are not properly housed. No one nation is immune from shelter problems. For Canada, which has seen substantial cut-backs to both international assistance and housing budgets this year, the ground that has been lost.
A government that stands today to celebrate an international day of shelter might also be called to account for some of the following issue which it alone has responsibility for: budgetary cuts for the one program which renovated housing for low income Canadians. The Rental Remedial Action Plan, a program which brought basic improvements to the rooming house and low-income rental housing and is vitally important in our cities, is now terminated. What will replace it? There is reduction of co-operative housing from the proposed target of 5,000 units per year, which was never attained, to a now paltry 1,700 units which is supposed to serve all of Canada. How can we tackle affordable housing this way? It is a crushing blow to housing affordability that present high interest rates and the future goods and services taxes will bring to Canadians. It is no overstatement to say that the goal of housing Canadians to a decent standard is receding despite our unparalleled affluence.
The government, in its wisdom, cannot even fund such worthy self-help projects as Project Beaver, an organization which has specialized in training people in rural and remote parts of Canada to house themselves. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Surrey North, who is our housing critic, is fond of saying that there is no housing problem for the wealthy in Canada. The market does provide everything beyond our wildest dreams but increasingly, the market which this government puts its faith in has nothing to offer in terms of affordable accommodation.
I wonder if this is to be our message to the world on World Habitat Day, put your faith in the magic of the market, and if that does not work, then hope for some charity. It is not the way forward that we in the New Democratic Party endorse. We will be pressing for a housing policy which will house all Canadians and one which will be an example to the world. That would be a
Routine Proceedings
goal worth striving for on succeeding World Habitat Days.

Mr. Speaker, I have the responsibility to table a petitions with regard to the impending announcement on VIA Rail and the savage cuts the government is proposing. These petitioners would like this House to consider the following.
The Government of Canada has decided to eliminate many of VIA Rail's existing routes and thousands of jobs. The people of Canada deserve a high quality passenger rail service, including modernized equipment throughout the network and a rapid rail system for the Windsor-Quebec City corridor. The Government of Canada, in acting in the way it is going to act in a few days to come, are indeed cutting into a very essential service. These petitioners pray and call upon Parliament to urge the Government of Canada to not cancel in whole or in part rail passenger services in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I too have the honour and duty to rise under Standing Order 36 to present several petitions containing several hundred names of constituents of mine from Brantford and Brant county, but also from other centres in southwestern Ontario, severely criticizing, indeed, condemning the

October 2, 1989
Routine Proceedings
government for even tampering with VIA Rail, let alone shutting it down to cities like Brantford.
At a town hall meeting yesterday afternoon, at which over 300 people turned out to a tri-level meeting, this petition was signed by many more people. The petitioners call upon the government not to terminate rail passenger service to Brantford, Woodstock and other communities in Ontario, but indeed to expand this environmentally-friendly and cost-effective means of transportation, if it was properly administered, properly funded and properly set up. Every other country is doing it. There is no reason why this country cannot do it.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to present a petition on behalf of the Canadian constituents across this nation who are violently objecting to the proposed cuts to VIA Rail. VIA Rail is an essential service to those rural communities across Canada. Older people depend on this to keep their medical appointments at hospitals, particularly from Sarnia to London and in other areas of Canada. The petitioners humbly call upon this Parliament to urge the Government of Canada not to cancel in whole or in part, rail passenger services in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to submit a petition signed by many Canadians who are voicing their opposition to the proposed goods and services tax and who say that the proposed tax is just unacceptable. They just cannot bear the increased taxation. Many small businessmen and women feel that their businesses not only cannot handle the new tax but cannot handle the cost to them of collecting the tax.

Mr. Speaker, in accordance with Standing Order 36, I am pleased to present a petition certified correct as to form and content and signed by dozens of constituents, ordinary Canadians, objecting to the government's intended plan to decimate VIA Rail. It is a pleasure to present this document on behalf of these petitioners.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to address the house considering the government's economic record, in particular our record on job creation. I welcome this opportunity because since this government took office Canadians have experienced a wide economic expansion combined with steadily decreasing unemployment that, despite what the prophets of doom and recession may say, the economic expansion shows no signs of letting up.
One reason we have succeeded in turning the economy around was that five years ago this government committed itself to economic renewal and to the sometimes difficult measures needed to effect change and generate growth. In short, we had and still have a coherent comprehensive economic game plan based on the direction Canada must go if our labour market is to succeed today and in the future defined by new skills and demands and growing international competition.
On the evidence it would seem that the government's blueprint to generate meaningful long-term economic change is proving to be the right one. The simple fact is
Supply
that since the government took office in September, 1984, unemployment in Canada has fallen from 11.6 per cent to 7.4 per cent and continues to fall. In this period the total employment has risen by 1,555,000 jobs and 87 cent of them are full-time jobs. More important, of all the new jobs created since 1984, 56 per cent have been filled by women.
When this government took office we recognized that youth employment was an area of particular concern, not only for our young people themselves but for the long-term health of the Canadian labour market. With this in mind the Minister of State for Youth has implemented far-reaching youth strategies with the provinces of New Brunswick and Newfoundland and is considering other initiatives to ease the transition of young people into the world of work.
On the broader front we have also successfully initiated two comprehensive agreements which have signalled a new era in federal-provincial economic co-operation. I am speaking of course of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency and the Western Economic Diversification agency. These two initiatives, along with the industrial adjustment service and the Community Futures Program, have established a co-operative, pro-active approach to dealing with inevitable industrial or sectoral adjustment. Their successes in revitalizing companies and communities and saving jobs is directly related to involving the very people affected- employers, union representatives and community groups.
This government understood from the outset that the long-standing regional disparities could no longer be addressed through the traditional piecemeal so-called make work programs administered from central Canada.
Over the past five years progress has been made to minimize these disparities and, while much remains to be done, the processes and the programs are in place along with a new spirit of co-operation to generate long-term regional growth. Since 1984, employment has risen in every province, by 19 per cent in British Columbia and by more than 10 per cent in seven other provinces.

October 2, 1989
Supply
Just as significant as the number of jobs for Canadians is the type of jobs they have been getting. Through the Canadian Jobs Strategy, which we introduced in 1985 as part of our long-term economic blueprint, almost
1.500.000	Canadians have received training and on the job experience. After participation in a Canadian Jobs Strategy project most have gone on to permanent employment in positions relevant to today's labour market needs.
Consistent with the mandate of the Canadian Jobs Strategy, the large majority of participants have been those Canadians who are most in need-women returning to the workforce, young people who are unemployed or underemployed, the disabled and native Canadians. By turning decision making and budgetary leverage over to the regions, Canadian Jobs Strategy programs are operating with maximum impact and cost effectiveness.
It is clear that Canadians are responding to what they perceive as a necessary and workable package of initiatives to bring about economic renewal. The Canadian Jobs Strategy is part of that package. Comprehensive tax reform to bring about a more competitive tax system, including the GST, is part of the package. The free trade agreement is also part of that package.
I should say at this point that sales tax reform could raise employment from the start and create more than
60.000	in the private sector. The opposition always talks about the 4,000 people they say will be added to the public roll. I say again that they say that; we do not say that it is 4,000. That is their estimate. The fact is that there will be at least 60,000 new jobs created by the GST in the private sector.
Statistics Canada labour force surveys released since the agreement was signed in January show that total employment has risen by 209,000 jobs so far this year. This growth, moreover, is reflected in almost every sector of the Canadian economy, including manufacturing, construction, agriculture, communications, trade and real estate.
And for those determined pessimists across the floor who insist on seeing, indeed it seems almost hoping for, an economic downturn, let me quote some more recent statistics if I may. Over the last period for which figures are available, July to August, 1989, employment was up again by 73,000 jobs, all of them full-time, shared among men, women, young people. And during this period
Quebec among all the provinces experienced the strongest growth. Obviously the remarkable expansion in the Canadian economy is not a temporary thing, but the government is determined to build on this growth, because we understand that to continue to prosper in the future a far-sighted approach to the skills requirements of our labour force and our labour market is needed.
In this regard the Minister of Employment and Immigration introduced an important initiative last spring designed to prepare our workforce for the future. I am referring to the labour force development strategy. As members of this House are aware our labour market is undergoing tremendous change. Canadian business and industry face challenges posed by technological change, expanding global markets and world competition. The labour force development strategy is part of the government's ongoing response to those challenges.
For the unemployed the strategy marks a significant shift away from passive income support toward programs and services which will help Canadians get working as quickly as possible. For those Canadians who do have jobs the priority will be to equip them with the skills the changing labour market demands. To do this we will be enlisting the involvement of the private sector, unions, educators and other groups as never before. Let me add that this involvement of Canadians from all sectors has been another cornerstone in our economic policy from day one.
It is the enterprise of Canadians that has fuelled and will continue to fuel our national economic renewal. The labour force development strategy is a massive and complex undertaking. I will not touch on the details at this time, many of which are still being worked out in consultation with Canadians from all sectors. But I will add that the strategy is fully consistent with our belief in long-term, fully integrated economic activity.
Canadians are well aware and appreciate this government's commitment to the economy and job creation. Our labour force development strategy underscores that commitment. By tackling the realities of a changing labour market we are working to ensure that Canadians will have the opportunities for productive employment in the 1990s and beyond. This and other contemporary economic issues are simply too large and crucial to address with the haphazard, stop gap programs of the past or programs that leave Canadian business and
October 2, 1989

industry on the sidelines when decisions must be made and policies developed.
The government recognized the need for long-term comprehensive planning when we took office in 1984. We recognize it today as we continue to take the necessary measures to build a foundation for economic success.

Madam Speaker, I would like to convey to the hon. member for Burlington that I listened with great interest to what he had to say. We have discussed this matter on several occasions.
I have two fairly simple questions. They are legitimate questions and are not made for any particular purpose. I would like to have the member's response if I may.
The first one is that to my knowledge the de Grandpre report, for which I think the government paid somewhere in the vicinity of $1.5 million to have completed, made a recommendation which was very much in keeping with the action that the government was taking, i.e., to combine the safety net of unemployment insurance with the trampoline offered in the sense of training. It was my understanding that we made that recommendation and that there were five members I believe on that committee; only one representative of labour, the rest were business. The recommendation was made that the training should be done but that the money should come out of a tax on business. I believe it was 1 per cent. I would like to know why that was not followed.
The second item is a legitimate question. I cannot understand why the government is getting out of unemployment insurance altogether in a very short time frame.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, what the hon. gentleman says is not quite correct. Bill C-21, which is another matter that we are going through in committee right now, puts a limit of 15 per cent on the amount of money that may be used for training. The balance of the training funds will come from the Canadian Jobs Strategy. I would venture to say there will be a lot more money paid out of the CJS than out of UI funds.
Supply
But that whole discussion is another argument that is being put forth by many people who comment on whether we should in fact use UI funds for training. When you boil it all down it is a matter of what you consider a benefit, whether benefits are just dollars or whether you can take someone who is presently contributing to the UI fund and becomes unemployed and use some of those funds to train him so that he can get back into the fund. In other words, benefits can be training as well as dollars. That is the legal opinion we have, and that is the way we are going to proceed in that regard.
The de Grandpre report had many things in it, some of which we agreed with and some we disagreed with. Consequently we did not put it all into effect. I think if we had we would have a larger howl from the members opposite than we have today with Bill C-21.
We are going to proceed with training, and that training is going to be supplemented by people in the areas and regions to indicate to us what training should be done there to enhance future employment of people who are presently unemployed.

Madam Speaker, I have never heard so much gobbledegook and tripe on this discussion as I have heard from the member opposite. I feel offended as a member of Parliament, especially when the member opposite quotes a whole series of Statistics Canada figures that have already been contested in committee, and I am going to have to do it again.
The lower unemployment rate to which he refers is still higher than that which was experienced in Canada prior to the recession. For six years prior to the recession we had a lower unemployment rate than we have now. For six years prior to the recession we had a higher employment rate than we do have now. Those are the kinds of figures the government is using to justify withdrawing from unemployment insurance, even though constitutionally the purpose of unemployment insurance is to provide income support for those who find themselves without jobs in a period of duress.
What the minister and the member opposite are trying to do is boondoggle Canadians into thinking that that money is actually going to go into training. That too is not true, especially when he quotes figures like 15 per cent. The 15 per cent of premiums, according to 1989

October 2, 1989
Supply
estimates, will net the government $1.8 billion. Last year and for 1989 estimates under CJS for job training programs, the government has slotted less than $800 million. It has cut $700 million over the course of the last four years.
The Conservatives expect us to believe that while they are cutting funds from training they are going to use moneys that are derived for insurance purposes and for income purposes for training. I do not think Canadians are that stupid. We are certainly not gullible.
The member opposite is perpetrating an absolute untruth when he talks about the constitutionality of using that 15 per cent of funding because first of all that 15 per cent of funding is going to net more moneys than they anticipated. It is a windfall that they are going to abuse, and I say that deliberately because there is already some legal opinion that that 15 per cent constitutes a complete and total fundamental change of the UI system.

If that was a short question I will give you an example of a very short reply.
When we took over the government in 1984 the UI fund was $4.5 billion in deficit. That has been repaid. It is now $500 million in surplus through fiscal 1989 and it will be $500 million in surplus after this year. What you have just said is total nonsense.

Madam Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to rise in the House today to speak on the motion of the member for Vancouver Quadra. It reads: "That this House condemns the government for its mismanagement of the Canadian economy", more specifically, the threat to impose a 9 per cent goods and services tax, high interest rates, negligence in the management of trade, abandonment of farming, fishing and forest industry and, finally, continued neglect of regional disparities.
I will first address the 9 per cent Mulroney sales tax. What we have here is a massive shift of responsibility from the federal government to individuals, to small business, to low income people, to our elderly and to other levels of government.
Let us first look at how this imposition will affect municipal government which of course the same taxpayer supports but from a different pocket. If I could I would like to refer to a brief submitted by the Federation of Canadian Municipalities to the minister of revenue.
The finance minister assured the Canadian municipalities that local government would not be used as a source of new revenue. The technical paper indicates that municipalities are to be rebated a substantial part of the remitted GST. But even so, there are considerable inequalities which cause a contradiction to the minister's over-all commitment.
According to the FCM report it is the failure of the proposed government formula to recognize the extraordinary administrative burden confronting municipalities under GST. There are several types of tax collection and remittance requirements to which they will be subjected. To name a few, they will be faced with the task of tracking the applications of any good or service acquired in order to determine the appropriate GST treatment, and the government formula will vary from municipality to municipality. Some municipalities will be winners and other municipalities will be losers.
Second, compensation for administrative costs applies to small business. Why not municipalities?
Third, cash flow costs are ignored while waiting for the rebate.
Fourth, the burden of a federal tax on top of a provincial tax will increase costs to municipalities beyond the amount recognized in the formula.
Fifth, the commitment of the Minister of Finance to municipalities was that services such as telephone systems, natural gas, hydro, water-they sell their water- would not be subjected to the tax increase, and yet the technical paper states the contrary. The Minister of Finance, in spite of that commitment to the municipalities, has reneged on all those commitments to those municipalities. Their only source of revenue is from the property tax base and whatever grants they are at the mercy to receive from the province and the federal government.
Government members have no one to blame but themselves when faced with a public that has nothing but doubt and cynicism over the government's true motives. First they said it would be revenue neutral then they said it would be visible. On both counts the government lied,
October 2, 1989

and therein lies the lack of trust the public has for this government.
Further, the government's misleading sales tax ad campaign shows contempt for Parliament and undermines the democratic process. Financially depressed regions of the country will be given not a double whammy but many, many whammies. First the 9 per cent GST, then a massive reduction in the federal government spending on regional development. Cut-backs on the UI program and transfer payments will be reduced to the provinces by one percentage point. Finally, those outlying regions will be the hardest hit with far higher transportation costs for all their goods.
High interest rates will go hand in hand with the GST and will for some time to come. Other ill effects will be higher taxes, higher inflation costs and fewer jobs. The government itself has admitted that the GST will raise inflation by two and a quarter per cent in 1991. We know that the Bank of Canada sets its interest rate by the inflation rate.
The GST will seriously affect trade in Canada. The Conference Board of Canada estimates that 72,000 jobs will be lost because of the GST.
My time allocation does not allow me to mention all the negative aspects of the GST, but is it any wonder that taxpayers are concerned?
The government has doubled tax revenues in five years, and yet has doubled the national debt in the same period of time. In addition, these five years were ones of unprecedented economic growth. The government earned billions of dollars in excess revenue over estimate in the past five years. What did it do with this money? It certainly did not go to reduce the deficit. This government has mismanaged the affairs of the country to such a horrendous measure that they are now panicking and moving forward to a disastrous GST.
I hope this government gains its senses before the citizens of this country revolt. The imposition of a 9 per cent sales tax, a consumption tax that will hurt those who can least afford it, is not acceptable or is a 7 per cent or a 5 per cent or a 3 per cent GST acceptable. This government must negate this whole plan and go back to
Supply
the drawing-board to find a more equitable way of replacing the manufacturers' sales tax.
I have a motion which I would like to put forward. Given the importance of this debate and given the great opposition to the GST and the number of people who wish to speak, I move, according to Standing Order 26(1):
That the House continue to sit during the lunch hour.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to stand here today and address the motion that we see before us, a motion that some of my friends opposite spoke to last week which gave me the opportunity to respond at that time.
If I could, what I would like, is to take this opportunity to speak in the inevitably short 10 minutes specifically on the fishery. The fishery is such a critical part, not only of my province of Newfoundland and Labrador but, indeed, of Atlantic Canada, parts of Quebec, certainly British Columbia and growingly, provinces in the areas that we do not traditionally consider part of the fishery. It is an industry that I would suggest is finally being recognized as a national industry. It is an industry that is important to all Canadians no matter where they live and whatever they do to make a living.
I am horrified by the motion we see before us which states:
That this House condemns the Government for the
mismanagement of the Canadian economy, including -
The relevant phrase here is:
-abandonment of Canadian primary producers with resulting
undermining of the farming, fishing and forestry industries;
Absolutely nothing could be further from the truth. This government has shown time and again that its concern is not only with those industries but the people and the communities that depend so heavily on those industries.

October 2, 1989
Supply
The policies of this government are focused on the long-term benefit, the long-term survival of these industries, of the fishery, to ensure that our people in our communities can depend upon a fishery that gives them a stable, a predictable and a worth-while remuneration for their efforts and which ensures the long-term benefit to those people and the long-term survival of those communities.
You cannot take short-term measures to exact longterm gain. There are no immediate responses to what is a complex and historical problem that has resulted from a myriad of a factors. We face in Atlantic Canada, and therefore in Canada generally today, an industry that looks towards some very difficult times, an industry that will demand consultation. It will demand imaginative and constructive public policy. It will demand strong response from government, from industry, from all of those who participate in and benefit from the fishery. It is that leadership that this government is and will provide to that fishery.
I look at the west coast in terms of the development of the Pacific salmon fishery. We had four good years of runs. We have gone from 13,000 metric tonnes in 1986 to
35,000	metric tonnes today. We have a strong shellfish and groundfish industry in western Canada, in British Columbia.
The free trade agreement panel is hearing the process there. Unfortunately, because of the death of one of the commissioners, there has been a problem. But with the appointment of Mr. Don Tansely who was a long-serving and is a well-recognized senior public servant that process will move ahead. This government has represented the interests of the British Columbia industry with vigour and determination.
The current situation in the Atlantic fishery has grown out of a number of interrelated and complex, scientific, economic, and historic factors. There are some things that we cannot control, such as exchange rates and lower margins of profit. But at the same time this government has moved ahead with a policy to address the problems in our fishery. That is specifically what I would like to discuss for a few minutes.
There are four cornerstones to that action. Particularly in recognition of this problem, the challenge that we all
face in dealing with the problems in the Atlantic fishery, the Prime Minister has appointed a special committee of cabinet, senior ministers from a variety of departmental backgrounds to address the problem that we face in dealing with the scientific results on the northern cod stock. That committee will look at exactly what the situation is. It will look at what the options are for all of us, be we government, the industry, or those who depend on the industry. Then, we will develop the response of this government and lead those participating in this debate, this consultation, in dealing with this issue to ensure that we have the stocks that are necessary to protect the long-term availability of the resource that we so fundamentally depend upon, particularly in Atlantic Canada.
Second, the special task force that has been set up to deal with the fishery in Nova Scotia, known as the Hache task force, is designed to examine the state of the fishery off the Scotia shelf. This task force has been consulting broadly with a number of people. There have been public hearings. Mr. Hache will report to the minister and his findings will be discussed by the special committee.
Third, the government has made the problem of foreign over-fishing a priority of the highest order. From the Prime Minister to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, to the Minister of Fisheries, to the Minister for International Trade we have made it clear to the Europeans that the ongoing overfishing is of a disastrous nature. It is of such serious concern to this government that it substantially affects the relationship between two very good friends. This diplomatic effort has been carried out with the European Community generally and with specific members of the European Community, as well as with the United States of America which too, in the past, has refused to honour the necessities of sustainable development and the necessities of protecting that resource. That process continues.
The fourth cornerstone of our policy, something that will benefit both the Pacific and the Atlantic fishery, is to take steps to strengthen fisheries management and to introduce amendments to the Fisheries Act to protect the resource. That will involve increasing deterrents and the effectiveness of enforcement, updating and strengthening fisheries management systems generally.

As I am sure you and my colleagues opposite well know, Madam Speaker, we have taken a number of actions already to deal with some of the these problems. Enforcement has been substantially increased along the 200-mile limit. Fines have been increased. Our ports remain closed. We have increased the spending on science, particularly in response to the Harris commission report, by 80 per cent. We are spending $3 million more to ensure that the science that is carried out now is as good as it can be and that areas that have not been dealt with in the past are dealt with in the future. That particularly relates to things like hydro-acoustics and oceanography.
I would like to talk briefly about the goods and services tax that we have heard so much about and how it relates to fishermen. Neither farmers nor fishermen will charge tax on their sales of food-related products. Fishermen will get back the tax that they pay on anything they buy to use to run their businesses in the prosecution of the fishery. In the past the tax has been payable and been accumulated and people have not seen it. Not only will the GST not apply to the fish they sell, but any of the tax they get back on boats, gasoline, nets or anything at all they use in the fishery will come back.
To conclude briefly, this government recognizes that the fishery in Atlantic Canada is an integral part of the economy of this country. Problems that are faced by the Atlantic fishery are problems that all Canadians share. The policy of this government is designed to directly address that today and in the future.

I have listened to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and a colleague from the Atlantic quite attentively. It amazes me that we can both represent a fishing area and come from the Atlantic yet we can both stand up in this House and declare that there is a very acute crisis in the fisheries on the east coast. Not only is it in fisheries, it is in other areas. It could be infrastructure because of VIA, or a decrease in air services or any of a multitude of areas.
I listened to his colleague talk about unemployment and what a great record their government has. The Member for St. John's East said, "There is nobody hurting in the fisheries. It is only a matter of different rates, the economies of scales, because the dollar has
Supply
gone up against the American. We are suffering that hardship".
The municipal leaders of three counties, Shelburne where his colleague the Member for South Shore comes from, Yarmouth and Digby, met this summer. They asked to meet with the Minister of Fisheries. They have not had an answer to their request, which was made over two months ago. They have had no recognition from the government opposite. They have not been able to meet with his minister, the minister to whom he is parliamentary secretary.
I say this because there is a hardship. I met a man who has fished for 38 years, 18 or 16 of them with his father and over 20 on his own. He has had seven weeks of employment. That is unheard of in southern Nova Scotia. It is absolutely incredible that in this year-because he had his boat in the boat shop-he has only fished seven weeks when we are there where the fish are and we see the Cape North 30 miles away.
Could the parliamentary secretary implore the Prime Minister to come down and meet with the people in Lockeport, meet with those people who are unemployed, meet with all the plant workers who have not worked for two and a half months this year and two months last year because of the policies of his minister on the fishery, because of the bad management plan? Will he look at the Hache report that he talks about and present the people who came before that commission to the cabinet committee? It is out of the minister's hands. When you set up a cabinet committee to look at the policies of a minister you have taken it away from the minister. It is up to that cabinet committee.
Would he, as a member from the east coast, ask the Prime Minister to act quickly to ease the hardship in the fishery, look at what is happening with many, many thousands of people? I think it is about 11,000 in those three counties who had work in the fisheries who are not working in the groundfishery because of the policies of his minister.
Would he ask the Prime Minister to go to Lockeport this week, Wednesday night, or the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans who we have not seen on the east coast? There is an east coast. I do not think he was there all summer. We were off all summer. We asked to meet with him. We have not seen him. Maybe the Parliamentary secretary could be sent to Lockeport on Wednesday night to go with his colleague from South Shore who has

October 2, 1989
Supply
to face those many unemployed people. Would he ask him?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first and foremost, I would like to correct one thing that my colleague opposite has said. She put words into my mouth. She claims that I have said that nobody is hurting in the fishery. I said no such thing. It would be folly to even think any such thing. I know, as she knows, that people are hurting in the Atlantic fishery. I know, as she knows, that there is the potential that a lot more people could hurt in the Atlantic fishery.
But I know, as perhaps she does not know, that there are not immediate, instant solutions. I also know that the people who understand the fishery, who know what the fishery is all about, recognize that there are no instant solutions. The problems that have emerged over years and years result from a variety of reasons, some of them management, some of them science, some of them caused by foreigners, some of them caused by ourselves. But our solutions will come only with a reasoned and reasonable, well-thought out, informed position to start from, and a concerned, conscientious approach to the problems over the longer term.
The hon. member opposite has no comer on concern and, clearly, no corner on knowledge of the fishery. This minister and this government have shown by reacting, by forming a cabinet committee, by appointing the Hache Commission, by dealing with the problem in a consensus-based, organized fashion, not by sitting bleating, putting words into other people's mouths.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The period for questions and comments is over. There is only five minutes and the hon. member for South West Nova took four of them.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre on debate.

Madam Speaker, the problem with fanaticism is that it blinds one to reality. It is unfortunate that the last member who spoke, a new member of the House who came in with great expectations, has so quickly been absorbed into that fanatical obsession that this government has had about its own peculiar way of managing the economy of Canada. It has blinded him and others to the hard reality
of what is taking place in this country. It is too bad that a gentleman who feels so passionate about his region is so blind to decisions taken by his government which are totally eroding the position of the fishing sector, the primary agricultural-forestry sectors of this country, not by some act of God's will, not by some long-term change in the atmosphere, but by direct decisions undertaken by ministers of his government over the last four or five years. These decisions have put the fishing sector in a precarious position. They are now doing the same with agriculture, and with all our primary producers, all our commodity sectors in the economy.
I put to the hon. member the simple but clear decision taken by his government under the free trade agreement to surrender the right of Canadians to apply export taxes to protect their own primary producers on processing. How does he get up and say that somehow someone made us do it when, in fact, it was the signature of his Prime Minister on that agreement that surrendered the one area that would provide, under the fish processing decision, the processing industry on the west coast and, ultimately, the east coast, the right to protect their own industry? It was not some far off, distant, foreign, unknown stranger who did it. It was his Prime Minister.
We now face a situation where we already have an interim report on the fish processing dispute on the west coast, where we clearly see where the decision will go, that the Americans are going to win the case. In the meantime we have given up. We have surrendered. We have voluntarily thrown away the legitimate means at our disposal to protect our processing industry.
Yet that member has the gall, the effrontery and the nerve to stand up and say, "It is somebody else's fault". Sir, it is your fault. It is your government's fault that the the fishery industry of Canada has been put in jeopardy. It is about time you started answering honestly for your responsibilities.
Hear, hear!

I say the same thing when you go to agriculture. Once again, we are pretending that somehow there is some far distant secret move afoot to undermine agriculture. Well, Madam Speaker, I point to you the decisions being taken in the

dairy industry. We talk about the fact that we now have a GATT decision saying we cannot use import controls.
That man of great integrity, the Minister of Agriculture and Deputy Prime Minister says, "Well, it has nothing to do with free trade. It is that GATT decision. What am I going to do about it?". What he forgets, and what the members opposite forget, is that during the debate on free trade, his predecessor, the former minister of agriculture got up and said, "Now, look it, I recognize that by taking the tariffs off on all these agricultural products, on food processing, on dairy products, that that will put our supply management system in jeopardy". Those were the words of the Hon. John Wise, former Minister of Agriculture. He said, "But I have a solution. I will give you a guarantee. I will put a control on imports of yogurt and ice cream." Well, we all said, "We do not think it is going to work, but let us give it a try".
They knew right from the start that that was a phoney, that that was a placebo, that that would disappear. Now it is being challenged and the government has no recourse. It knows that the entire supply management system of Canadian agriculture is under attack. They say, "We did not have anything to do with it". It was their signature on that agreement. They put their name on the document. They knew full well what they were doing. Now they put the entire dairy industry-in fact the entire supply management system-under jeopardy.
Similarly, let us take the pork decision. Once again, we on this side of the House said, "Now, wait a minute. What the free trade agreement is going to do when it is signed is entrench into law U.S. trade requirements. We are going to have to administer U.S. trade law". The Americans, who are pretty smart and shrewd about these things, slipped in the new law last summer, the omnibus trade bill. They rewrote their trade law just before the free trade agreement came into being. They rewrote the definition of what a subsidy is. They rewrote what we could do. So we signed the agreement. The Prime Minister stands up flag-waving, bands beating, saying alleluia, it is a great day for Canadian agriculture. In the meantime, knowing that what we have signed ourselves to is a sentence which says that we can no longer have agricultural stabilization programs, or regional development programs, or agricultural support programs. It is no
Supply
longer allowed because the free trade agreement, inscribing as it does U.S. trade law, prevents it. Now, there is all this fuss and bother, "We have got to go to the GATT again".
I recall during the election campaign as I debated across the country with the Hon. John Crosbie said, "You know, the reason why Canadians should accept the free trade agreement is because we do not have to worry about the GATT any more. It is going to give us secure, guaranteed access to the U.S. markets".
Now, when we get into trouble, who are they running off to? We had better go back to our old friends, the GATT. What a difference a couple of months makes.
It is no wonder the minister does not want a report card. Because under that report card, whoever would be authorizing it would not only fail the minister, they would send him back for remedial training. The fact of the matter is they knew what they were doing. At the same time in agriculture they were saying, "Well now, we are going to protect all of these agricultural programs". Yet, they had put together their own position paper at the GATT, under the Uruguay round, suggesting that they were going to negotiate away all these subsidies. There it is in their own documents that they tabled in Geneva. They now think we have to renegotiate all this.
The Hon. Member gets up and says, "Hey, we are doing everything we can for the primary producers in this country". They are the forgotten people in this country. They are the ones who feel that this government does not speak for them. There is no voice, there is no one to listen, they simply ignore them.
Of course, when you come down to the fundamental question as to why a lot of this is happening, let us talk for just a moment about the interest rates in this country and the exchange rate that goes along with it. I put on the floor of this House, Madam Speaker, this direct charge and I want the government to answer it. As part of the negotiation, as a side part, while the minister and others were off negotiating free trade, the Minister of Finance was off negotiating with his American counterparts an understanding that we would substantially increase the exchange rate on the Canadian dollar. That was part of the deal. It was not written in words, but that

October 2, 1989
Supply
was part of the deal. That is the reason why, right now, that we sit with an 85-cent dollar.
It is why in the last report from Stats Canada, exports in this country nosedived by 8 per cent. We now have a maximum of $127 million surplus in our trade account. That is the lowest in ten years. We are almost at the point of running a deficit in our trade account. That is no accident. It is no coincidence. It does not happen by some manipulation amongst the gods. It happens directly. One of the prices we are paying, a consequence of our new economic relationships, is the fact that we now have the highest point spread on interest rates in the history of this country and an exchange rate which has no basis in the economy whatsoever, except the fact that we made a deal. As a result, whether you are a fisherman, a farmer or a lumber producer, you are paying the price.
On Friday afternoon I quoted in this House figures from British Columbia which pointed out that the profit margin in the softwood lumber industry of British Columbia fell from a high in 1987, $357 million to $6 million in 1988. That is a direct consequence, a direct result of this government's signature on a piece of paper with the Government of the United States.
How often can we have members from the opposite side stand up and somehow pretend that our export market is dropping in a barrel, that primary producers are losing their markets, losing their protection, losing their supply-management, losing their right to market, that all these things are an act of will? There is only one place where the responsibility must be carried and that is on the government opposite. It put their finger on the button. The government signed the paper. It is about time that it gives up this fanatical obsession with the goods and services tax which will only exaggerate the problems all the more, and got back to some serious management of this economy so that once again we can show our primary producers in this country that they are not the forgotten people of Canada.

Madam Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague for Winnipeg South Centre for refocusing on the free trade agreement, which I understand the government no longer wishes to talk about. The government suggests that it has won the public relations battle and are into a new public relations battle, the goods and services tax. So, it is important that we refocus again on
the free trade agreement and report cards should be issued. Indeed, it will be labelled a failure.
On the rulings that are going to come before the panel in the not too distant future, it would appear that we are going to lose the fishing ruling.
Very important to my constituency is the steel rail ruling which one year from now I understand, in all likelihood, we will lose. Despite the fact that there is an airtight case, there is every indication that it is an unwarranted, illogical, ridiculous, no proof kind of a judgment by the commerce department of the United States. They are suggesting that there is no basis in fact for the ruling, but it is likely to injure the Canadian steel producers in the future. But, nevertheless, application of American trade law suggests that in fact we will probably lose that ruling as well.
I would ask the member for Winnipeg South Centre, given his free trade expertise, what would his reaction be should we lose both of these rulings? Were he given the opportunity to act, what alternatives would he take?

I suppose the opportunity is one that we clearly stated during the election campaign. We have to get rid of a deal that sells out Canada. That is the starting point.
Unfortunately, what we have found in this deal-and now it is coming home to roost-is that it is skewered against us. The member just pointed out the decisions on steel, on pork and on other areas. The fact of the matter is that what FTA requires us now to do is basically implement U.S. trade law. They changed their law. They rewrote their law to give them the advantage. Therefore, we have substantially weakened our ability to make claims in the international circles, in the international tribunals.
The GATT panel on pork, on dairy products, or steel, is going to say: "Hey, Canadians, you were consenting adults. You got into this relationship with the United States. You knew what you were doing. Don't ask us to bail you out of a bad relationship, a bad deal". All of a sudden we will be forced into a position where-we could normally have referred these kinds of questions and got a reasonably objective decision-we have to recognize now as Canadians that every decision taken at the GATT will be substantially influenced by the existence of the free trade agreement. It is there and it will set the tone. Furthermore in many cases it will supersede
October 2, 1989

any GATT decisions. Therefore, we may get a decision on pork favourable to us under the GATT, but it would not apply to the United States because of the free trade agreement.
We will be forced into a position where we are the odd person out. We will be standing out as one of the eccentrics in the world of international trade because of that agreement. It puts us in a perpetual inferior relationship in gaining proper secure guaranteed access to world markets and to the American market. Clearly, as we said right from the outset, it is time for Canadians to take a hard look at what they got themselves into and take a hard look at how we can get out of it.

I thank the hon. member for his wise comments. Is he aware that the American wheat growers are also planning to file a request under section 409(b) of the free trade agreement that could lead to a countervail by the U.S. administration against Canadian wheat farmers? Canadian wheat farmers have always grown and traded fairly. Is the member aware of that?
Could he tell me whether or not, given that we have seen the Americans retaliate recently on pork and given that we have seen the decisions regarding the dairy industry, he feels that in fact the government knew what it was doing when it signed this free trade agreement? Were they merely trying to mislead Canadians, or did they actually know what they were doing prior to signing the free trade agreement?

I am never sure that this government knows what it is doing, certainly when one considers its track record. I can tell you what it has done. By becoming involved in that agreement it has put the prairie regions, and in fact the wheat growing and grain growing areas of the entire country, in a position where we are going to lose the structures that we have taken 50 years to build .1 am speaking of the Canadian Wheat Board marketing systems, two-price wheat system, all those areas where we have carefully moulded a framework in which we could ensure price stability and active marketing of our products. They are now the number one targets of the United States. Of course what happens, again going back to the U.S. trade legislation, is that they gave themselves new
Supply
weapons to use which we did not and which we in the opposition warned about.
For example, Durum wheat farmers had the Department of Commerce doing their research for them. They are now getting free assistance from their government and all we get from our government is standing on the sidelines in a fit of absent-mindedness while those kinds of attacks upon the basic structure of our wheat growing areas go on.

Madam Speaker, it is my pleasure to participate in the debate today of the opposition motion. In part, the Liberal motion states:
That this House condemns the government for its mismanagement
of the Canadian economy, including-
5) continued neglect of regional disparities.
I do not agree with that statement in its entirety. What this government has done is not just neglect regional disparities, but it has gone on an outright campaign to attack the regions of this country. Nothing is a greater example than what it is doing with rail passenger services.
I want to spend a few moments going through the list of routes that every document that we have seen would suggest that the government is going to cut. It is my understanding that those cuts will be announced later this week. Let us start with Atlantic Canada, an area of the country that I have been spending a fair bit of time in learning how it is different and how it is similar to the area that I come from and seeing from riding the train there and talking to people the direct impact that these cuts will have.
For example, the Halifax to Sydney run currently accommodates 102,000 people every year; an incredible number of people using a very small and antiquated train, a train that we gave up in the central corridor years ago. They have got our hand-me-downs, but 102,000 people are using it.
When I talked to the people I found out why they were using the train. From Sydney alone there are over 10,000 men and women, but primarily men, who must go to Halifax for worker's compensation reasons, either for assessment, treatment, or for rehabilitation. Ten thousand people a year use that train. This government, in its wisdom, is going to force those people on to the highways of Nova Scotia, highways that are becoming ever crowded with major trucks including the haulage of coal,

October 2, 1989
Supply
becoming less safe, less sensitive to their needs in terms of injured workers. Thousands more take the train to go to Halifax for medical care unrelated to on the job injuries.
Throughout the whole Atlantic, the Atlantic route itself, 267,000 people a year use that train.
The Deputy Prime Minister told the people of Atlantic Canada a few years ago: "Use it or lose it". He gave them a target of 200,000 riders for the year 1990. Two years ago they met that target and now they are exceeding it. They used it, but now this government wants them to lose it.
The other interesting aspect of the Atlantic region is that 20 per cent of the passengers who use the Quebec City to Windsor corridor come off the Atlantic. It is fine and good to say that we will keep the corridor, but there are 20 per cent of the corridor passengers who will not be coming by train. The chances are they will not be continuing by train, but they will have been forced into using the air or bus modes and more than likely will be driving their cars.
The Halifax to Yarmouth line, 47,000 people; the Moncton to Edmundston line, 10,000 people. Clearly, a vast majority of the people of Atlantic Canada use the train on a regular basis. But, instead of providing them with the equipment that will make their riding more comfortable, instead of ensuring that they have the money to do the proper marketing to attract more and more tourists into Atlantic Canada, not just from the New England states but from Europe and from Asia, this government is going to pull the plug on the Halifax to Sydney run, the Halifax to Yarmouth run, and the Moncton to Edmundston run.
Even the Ocean Limited train that travels the North Shore, which is a very scenic route, is going to be reduced to three times weekly. It is ideal for the tourist trade, but because of the meandering nature of the trackage it is not designed to move people from point a to point b in a reasonable length of time. It will see a decline in usage, which I am sure is what the government wants, and in three or four years from now, if they get their way on this one they will say that people were not using it, our deficit is too high, so we are going to have to cut it.
Let me skip to the other end of the country to British Columbia and Alberta. This weekend on Vancouver Island the one hundred and third anniversary of the E & N Line was celebrated. As a passenger service, it is 103 years old. That line, the only line on Vancouver Island, is to be eliminated by this government in spite of the fact that I am told that it was part of the agreement between British Columbia and Canada when British Columbia joined Confederation. Therefore, there may be more that will happen if the government tries to go through with its plan.
On that line 45,000 people a year use that train. I am told by my colleagues from Vancouver Island that that is in spite of the fact that it goes the wrong way at the wrong time of day. Instead of providing a service from the northern parts down to Victoria so that people can come into Victoria for cancer treatments or for economic reasons, it goes the other way. We think it should do both, so that we are using the service as a tourist facility to take people throughout the island but at the same time take the residents of the island into Victoria for the business they have to concern themselves with. But 45,000 people are already using it.
In northern British Columbia the Jasper to Prince Rupert run is going to be reduced to a summertime operation only. This shows once again that this government does not understand the nature of rail transportation in this country. They will quickly point and say: "But those people along that line have other modes of travel. They have air, roads". The people who are saying that are people who drive around in chauffeured limousines on major expressways or who fly in a government plane somewhere. They do not understand that in the wintertime in some of these smaller communities along that line you take your life in your hands getting into a car and driving some place because of the treacheries conditions that exist there, particularly for senior citizens who have driven for years but now recognize that they would like to stay around on this earth a while longer and feel that it is better for them to ride the rails. They are not going to have that option any more.
That is no different from what this government is going to do to my region of the country in northwestern Ontario. The historic Canadian is also the only rail transportation around the north shore of Lake Superior. It parallels the Trans-Canada Highway, a highway where we literally kill dozens of people every winter in automobile accidents. The people in Terrace Bay, Schreiber, Rossport, White River, and all along the north shore, at least today and so far for the first part of this winter, will
October 2, 1989

have the option of catching the Canadian into Thunder Bay. But thanks to this government they will lose that option. Most of them do not have air transportation as an option, so the only recourse they have is to use the bus or an automobile, and studies have shown that people will use an automobile before they use a bus.
Clearly this fundamental destruction of rail passenger service in this country is an attack on the regions, even in southern Ontario, which will do okay because the corridor will be saved. My colleague, the member for Brantford spoke this morning when he was tabling petitions. His community is going to lose VIA Rail service. The community of Havelock will lose VIA Rail service. From the community of Niagara Falls, all the way up to Toronto, including Hamilton, will be served by Amtrak. How ludicrous, or is it?
Is it all part of that grand design that started with deregulation and then free trade to allow the Americanization of our transportation services? Freight railroads have running rights up into Canada now. Now Amtrak is going to come up to Toronto. Not just like it does in Montreal to make the connection with the American system, which makes a lot of sense, nor like it did when the corridor train at Windsor becomes an Amtrak train to provide that connection into the States, but this is to provide service within Canada. That is our job. It is our job to provide that service.
The impact on the regions will be devastating. We know that in tourism alone, passengers who use VIA Rail who are tourists from outside the country spend in excess of $600 million a year. That will be gone. That will not be replaced by some entrepreneur who will pay an arm and a leg to use CN or CR
I could go on and on. It is a subject dear to my heart, almost as dear as it is to the member for Regina-Lums-den. In conclusion, we will not give up. We are going to fight this to the bitter end.

What we are hearing is a recitation by members opposite of tax increases and expenditure reductions and the suggestion that there is something inherently wrong with that twin thrust. Surely it is time for a little bit of back to basics reality in this country.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the input from the opposition member who suggests that it has been doubled in the last five years. Yes, it has, because of the effect of compound interest on Liberal overspending. I challenge the members opposite when it comes time to question me to ask me about the composition of that debt, and I will be very happy to respond to you. I challenge you to do so.
I think it is clear to most reasonable Canadians-not to the opposition but to most Canadians-that we have to take in more revenue and spend less. That is the only way we are going to dig ourselves out of the economic mess which we have in this country.
Yes, Madam Speaker, taxes have increased. Unlike our profligate predecessors, however, we are spending far less on government programs than we take in in revenue at this point in time.
A number of other significant measures have been undertaken. Approximately 12,000 positions have been taken out of the federal bureaucracy, thus reducing its size to approximately the level it was back in 1973. There has been privatization of a number of non-essential Crown corporations, and I think here about enterprises like de Havilland and Canadair, which as Crown corporations were a continual millstone around the necks of the

Supply
Canadian taxpayers. They have been sold off the private sector and are flourishing today, employing more people than ever before. There is no reason why government has to own these enterprises. A government that can tax and can regulate surely has no need to own these things.
There have been further measures taken. The budget of this spring is the impetus for this debate. Yes, there are government spending reductions. They have been mentioned here: VIA, various military bases, CBC, other programs. How on earth can you reduce government spending if you do not eliminate some programs? It seems quite obvious to this side and to most rational Canadians that there has to be a response to the debt and the deficit problem, the cause of which I think we all know.
In addition to the measures that have been set out, tax reform is an important factor. It is part of our program whereby we are going to discipline spending and reduce the deficit. Sales tax reform means that the goods and services tax will replace the existing federal sales tax. There is nothing new about it at all. There has been a federal sales tax in this country since 1924. For 65 years Canadians have been paying a sales tax and it is a lot of money-$17 billion in federal revenue coming in this year as a result of the federal manufacturers' sales tax. That is the second largest source of revenue which the federal government has, and obviously it must be replaced by something else.
There is only one thing that all parties agree on in this House, and that is the recommendation that the existing federal manufacturers' sales tax is fundamentally flawed and therefore ought to be replaced. The finance committee unanimously passed a motion last year saying exactly that. Therefore, the Minister of Finance, quite responsibly, has brought forward a proposal for a goods and services tax. Thank goodness it has prompted debate in the country. For the first time many Canadians are becoming aware of the fact that there is a sales tax in existence, that it gathers in a lot of money, but it is hidden and people do not know about it. The more debate, the more discussion, and the more consultation we have about it the better. The proposal is out there.
There are some people who are saying that perhaps the base for this sales tax ought to be broadened. There are people who say to eliminate basic food, keep it out of there. They are the same people now who hypocritically
are criticizing government in the grey areas of take-out food and restaurants versus basic food.
Either you tax everything, or if you narrow the base you are going to have problems with exemptions. That is common sense but certainly I suggest not worthy of criticism from the people opposite.
Under the current federal sales tax we have four rates: 9 per cent, 11 per cent, 13.5 per cent, and as high as 19 on some goods. We are taxing the business inputs of our domestic companies while our foreign competitors are not similarly handicapped. This puts our companies at a major marketing disadvantage, both at home and abroad. That costs us jobs.
In addition, for most products the import price on which the tax is calculated does not include the foreign manufacturers' costs of marketing and distribution, while the price on Canadian manufacturers' products generally does. The result is that on average the tax paid on most taxable Canadian products is fully a third higher than the tax on competing imports. The importer pays less tax and thus can charge less. That makes us less competitive and it also costs us jobs. That, of course, is why the Minister of Finance has referred to the existing federal sales tax as a silent killer of jobs. That is why I believe most responsible Canadians, and indeed the opposition parties as well, have suggested that that tax has to go, that it should be replaced.
Other industrialized nations have recognized today's economic realities and have changed their tax systems accordingly. No other industrialized nation, with the exception of Canada, continues to have a manufacturers' sales tax. Why would we want to continue to shoot ourselves in the foot?
The first proposals for changing the federal sales tax were made back in the early 1940s. There are all sorts of problems with it. What to do about it? Why introduce a GST?
First, it will contribute to the deficit reduction effort and help ensure that we can continue to pay for the programs and services that Canadians value. Second, the GST is an essential element of this government's plan to make the changes necessary to ensure that Canada can compete in the modem world. The GST will fully remove federal sales taxes from the production process in Canada. It will reduce the cost of investment and improve the ability of Canadian producers to compete both in foreign markets and against imports from other countries. The GST will end the anomaly of a tax system
October 2, 1989

that favours foreign producers over Canadian businesses on our home turf.
There are some 750,000 small businesses in this country. They are the key, the generator, the engine for economic growth. They are the ones who have responded positively to the policies of this government and have expanded their businesses and created new ones with the result that there are over 1.5 million more Canadians working today than was the case five years ago. I salute the small business entrepreneurs, small business investors in this country, because they are the people who are responsible for that incredible record growth.
These businesses will be able to claim input tax credits to get back the tax paid on the purchases that they require for their businesses. They will simply deduct the tax paid on their purchases from tax owing on sales and remit the difference in each filing period. This will ensure that all tax is totally removed from inputs in the production process.
There will be a suggested threshold so that businesses with sales of less than $30,000 can choose to be in the GST system or not. There are streamlined accounting procedures ready. The government will help out with compliance costs. There will be assistance to businesses that wish to purchase more sophisticated point of sale equipment in order that they can write these expenses off for tax purposes. They will receive an administration fee to assist them in the remittance process. All of these measures are designed to keep compliance costs down and increase fairness between small and big business.
Third, it is a fair tax. There are some who have suggested that it is regressive. I fail to understand this. I think it is a knee-jerk reaction from those who have nothing better to do than criticize this government, no matter what. Surely a tax where the more you spend the more you pay is the fairest possible tax, the consumption tax. The people who have money spend more and pay more tax. Those with less income, lower income families, will be protected through a generous refundable tax credit in order to shelter them. It seems to me an eminently fair and progressive tax.
Supply
The GST is an essential part of this government's plan to build a stronger economy for Canada, an economy which is not overburdened with a massive debt and debt service charges which threaten future growth and our ability as a country to withstand changes in world economic conditions.
It will improve the fairness of the over-all tax system by putting in place measures to protect lower and modest income Canadians. The benefits of sales tax reform will be substantial, the GST will result in higher incomes and a higher standard of living for all Canadians. It is the right thing to do and that is why this government is proceeding with it.
