Madam Speaker, it certainly is a privilege to be back in Parliament and I appreciate the opportunity today to speak to the motion that is before the House.
Contrary to what the member across has just said, the state of the Canadian economy at present and the effects that a myriad of government proposals will have on Canadians for years to come is certainly not a pleasant theme to address.
As I travelled through my constituency of Hillsborough and other regions of Canada this summer, I was inundated with a barrage of complaints from the average hard-working Canadian. People are furious with the government for trying to impose upon them a completely new and unfair tax system. They are furious with the destruction of their national rail system. They are furious with the proposed changes to the unemployment insur-

ance program. They say, "What right does the government have to take 15 per cent of the workers' contributions to UI given in good faith and use them for retraining programs that are the government's responsibility to provide?"
My home province of Prince Edward Island is reeling from the economic impact of the CFB Summerside closure. No solutions or alternatives have been offered or even suggested to them. And how will they recover and replace this massive loss? And will they ever recover from the sense of betrayal and alienation?
All of the government initiatives outlined in today's motion are playing havoc with an already vulnerable economic base in various regions of Canada. I submit that the future is especially bleak in Atlantic Canada where deep regional disparity already abounds. Prince Edward Islanders, Newfoundlanders, New Brunswickers and Nova Scotians do not mind paying their fair share, but in return they deserve and expect fair treatment from their government. They have received none. ERDA, ARDA, DREE and ACOA moneys barely began to address the problem, and now even they have been slashed. Does this government believe that people can live on salt water alone?
According to an Industry, Science and Technology Canada document entitled Regional Disparity in Canada 1989, and using their definition of deep disparity as: "Below 70 per cent of the Canadian average of earned income per capita", Newfoundland had the highest rate of deep disparity in Canada at 95 per cent; and Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick were next at 50 per cent in 1987. These numbers remained unchanged from the previous year.
These numbers represent more than one million Atlantic Canadians who are living below the Canadian average of earned income. These statistics are quite startling. What is interesting about these numbers is that the government continues to hide behind the claims of
Supply
creating 1.5 million jobs since September of 1984. What we are asking is, where are all these jobs located?
What we have in Atlantic Canada is more than one million taxpayers who have to maintain an existence on incomes well below the national average. These people are subjected to the same government proposals that are dipping into pockets all over Canada. Canadians in the Atlantic region and elsewhere have been telling me and trying to tell their government that they have had enough.
The government definition of a sound fiscal policy has left us with a total public debt that has doubled in just five short years. After increasing our taxes some 31 times, this government now wants Canadians to dig deeper to pay for its disastrous handling of the economy. At the same time we are losing more and more services and social programs.
Now we are presented with the government's newest magic trick, the goods and services tax. What arrogance, Madam Speaker, to assume that Canadians will fall for this and that they will believe it is a better system when things are only getting worse for the average Canadian.
As the hon. Leader of the Opposition stated last Thursday in the House, Canadians have fraudulently been told that they will be taxed at a lower rate when actually it will be higher. We all know that this tax will not be revenue neutral and that it will not be visible. The tax will not be visible but the hardships that it will create certainly will be.
What is clear and visible to everyone but this government is that Canadians will not be fooled by the latest rabbit pulled out of the hat. We have been told many times over the past five years that our economy is booming. The growth should have improved the government's fiscal situation. Over the same period of time billions of dollars have been slashed from public spending by this government. Yet we are now told that we need a new consumption tax to reduce the deficit.
The GST is nothing more than an unprecedented plunge into the pockets of ordinary Canadians. These people will be hit by higher taxes, higher inflation, higher interest rates and fewer jobs. It would cause chaos in the business community and create a paper nightmare for small business. Over 82,000 small and medium-sized businesses, as members of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, are opposed to the imposition of the GST.

Let us touch briefly on how the proposed GST would affect the average working Canadian family. The Minister of Finance was quoted in thtlFinancial Post? on September 19, 1989 as saying: "Families earning less than $30,000 a year will be better off under the tax". The great favour being granted to these working families by the minister is the enhanced refundable sales tax credit.
I would like to relate some statistics that were presented to the Standing Committee on Finance by the National Council on Welfare in a submission entitled Help Wanted: Tax relief for Canada's poor. Their analysis found that single parents with incomes in the $10,000 to $15,000 range paid approximately $388 in federal sales tax in 1984. In 1991 even with the sales tax credit taken into account, these low-income families would still end up paying about $553 in net GST.
That is 42 per cent more than they paid in 1984. The reality is that the poorer families will be worse off in 1991 if the GST comes to fruition. They will be worse off than they were before the various so-called reforms of the past five years. By 1992 they will be in even more desperate shape, because inflation will begin to gnaw away at those much-lauded tax credits.
Everyone in this House knows that almost 80 per cent of the Canadian population is opposed to this sales tax. Can that many individuals be wrong, while the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister are right? Only the most arrogant would think so. I could give an entire litany on individuals and organizations that have studied and researched the GST, including groups in my own riding with which I have met. They all give the same reasons for opposing this so-called tax reform.
I say, and my colleagues on this side of the House say to this government: scrap this deal and come back with a better tax plan, one that Canadians can live with.
Given that I have only a few more minutes, I would like to speak briefly on the proposed changes to the unemployment insurance plan. Once again, this government is trying to put the boots to the ordinary Canadian worker. Specifically, these UI changes will have a disastrous impact on the Atlantic economy and especially on Prince Edward Island. As you are undoubtedly aware,
the workforce on P.E.I. is predominantly employed in seasonal operations-tourism, farming and fishing. Thus, unemployment insurance forms an integral part of our province's income profile.
Unemployment insurance was established as a no fault insurance program. It is a safety net and one that workers readily pay into for their protection in case they lose their jobs. I would like to cite an incident that occurred in my riding a few weeks ago. The members of the UI committee that were in Charlottetown heard this from a group that appeared before them.
A worker at a construction site collapsed with an apparent heart attack. An ambulance was called, but the fallen worker did not want to go to hospital. His reason was that he needed the week's work to ensure that he would qualify for benefits. Many employees do not have sick leave coverage or long-term disability plans. Thus they are forced to work when they really should seek medical attention. Their only recourse is to stay at work until they qualify for UI benefits. Now, with the proposed changes a worker will have to put in more weeks to qualify for fewer benefits.
Another concern with the proposed UI changes is the reallocation of $1.29 billion to job training programs. This proposal can only be seen as a slap in the face to Atlantic Canadians. What can Prince Edward Islanders be retrained for that will allow them the opportunity- the right-to continue working and living in their home province?
The bottom line is that they will be paying into a program that will force them to migrate to central Canada to find employment, thus continuing the erosion of the social and economic structure of our province. Our region of Canada is unique. It is unique because of its high unemployment, seasonal work and low wages. The government has failed to recognize this fact and continues to refuse to implement full employment programs which would offer meaningful, long-term employment in the Atlantic region. It makes little sense to force people into job retraining when there are no jobs to move into. What Atlantic Canada really needs is an adequate labour force development strategy. Until then we need to keep the unemployment insurance program as it is.

The present rate of unemployment in P.E.I. is 14.1 per cent. I do not see much prospect for improvement. The government should be advocating more flexibility and increased benefits to reflect the tough economic times that Islanders must face. Atlantic Canadians await proof that this government recognizes and respects their special needs. We have seen none thus far.
In conclusion, I support the motion by the Leader of the Opposition and I call upon members of this House to listen to their constituents, to condemn the government for its destruction of the socioeconomic system that Canadians built, and thus for its betrayal of the people themselves.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is with pleasure that I rise to speak on this motion that we are debating today. I am proud that this government is committed to building a strong economy, an economy which is competitive with the world's trading nations.
In order to achieve this goal, we must create a solid base on which to allow our economy to flourish in the coming years. Measures which seek to control the deficit and. reduce the national debt are an essential element of this foundation for the future. Equally, measures which seek to establish a sound, fiscal framework to sustain continued economic development are also essential to our purpose. These objectives are reflected in this government's commitment to a sound transportation policy.
Transportation is and always will be at the heart of our nation's economy. That is why we have undertaken to provide Canadians with a safe, effective and efficient transportation system. This system is the core around which our policy of economic regulatory reform was built.
With the advent of free trade, the role played by transportation in our economic development has become increasingly vital as we enter the next decade and the next century. A cost effective transportation system is essential if Canada is to preserve and enhance its position in world trade.
In order to meet this challenge we must make the best use of each mode of transportation: air, rail, marine, car, truck and bus. Continued subsidization of a mode of transportation which costs more and more and is used less and less is not a sound investment in our future, particularly when that investment is being made with the
Supply
Canadian taxpayers' money. That is exactly the situation we are facing with respect to our national rail passenger network.
VIA Rail's subsidy rose to an unprecedented $644 million in 1988. This translates into an average subsidy of $100 for every passenger that used the system.
We are asking all Canadians to pay this subsidy, but only 3 per cent of the travelling public uses this mode of transportation. Canadians have demonstrated their preference for other modes of transportation. With a market share of 84 per cent, the automobile is clearly the mode of choice.
Contrary to all the rhetoric which has been bandied about in recent months, VIA Rail's performance is worsening. It is not improving. While 1988 revenues did increase by 13 per cent or $26 million, operating costs increased by 15 per cent or $94 million, with the result that government subsidies to VIA for its operations alone had to be increased by $68 million. This means that for every additional dollar earned by VIA in 1988, the government has had to dispense an additional $2.62. So, for every dollar of additional revenue we spend $2.62 more.
Now the NDP, in their economic model, say because the revenue is better in itself then you should keep it, but they never mention the costs that are associated with that. That is the logic that they are putting forth in this argument.
As you can see, prompt action had to be taken to stop this drain on the public purse. That is why the government announced a new policy approach for VIA and asked the corporation to prepare a new business plan which would reflect its new reference levels. VIA was asked to consider all options that would allow it to operate within its budget, including such actions as fare increases, route abandonments, reductions in services on some routes and the take-over of services by private parties.
The government, however, does recognize that in a country as large and as diverse as ours there are some truly isolated communities which do not have access to any other mode of transportation. In order to meet this need, nine routes in five provinces will be maintained and subsidized. VIA Rail's corporate plan is currently under consideration and an announcement will be made in due course. The government expects the financial and

October 2, 1989
Supply
operation performance of VIA to improve and to function in a more cost effective manner.
This government has distinguished itself during the past four years through fiscal responsibility and judicious allocation of federal financial resources. When money is scarce it is spent where it is most needed, where it is most likely to produce results.
I invite the members opposite and indeed all Canadians to look at the facts and to judge for themselves the validity of the fiscal realities under which we currently labour. If we have had to make difficult decisions, it is because in 1984 we inherited a legacy of debt. This is a legacy that I personally do not care to pass on to my children and to their children. The difficult choices we have had to make allowed us to reduce the rate of growth of the deficit and bring the rate of inflation down to a more acceptable level.
Responsible fiscal management combined with sound economic policies have paved the road to a rate of economic growth which ranks among the highest in the industrialized world.
As responsible Canadians, we owe it to our children to leave them with every opportunity for development that we ourselves have enjoyed, and I am committed to working toward that end as part of the Government of Canada in 1989.

Madam Speaker, I rise today to speak on behalf of my constituents, small business, all those who will not get the opportunity to appear before the finance committee and who will not be allowed to express their outrage at the proposed goods and services tax. This government was first elected in 1984 in large part because of the Prime Minister's promise of tax reform.
It was argued, with some justification, that Canadians were being unfairly taxed and that the burden of financing government services was poorly distributed across the tax base. The Prime Minister sold himself as the great economic manager, the hero of big business. Five years later Canadians now realize that the Prime Minister has doubled the national debt, introduced crippling and regressive taxation policies and has launched an all-out assault on the pocketbooks of the middle class.
Now in 1989 we have begun to realize the Prime Minister and his colleagues in finance have a far different notion of tax reform than the rest of us. Over the summer I distributed a survey sheet in my riding and asked constituents what they felt were the most important issues facing the country today. I assumed, perhaps naively, that the responses would be primarily about abortion, Meech Lake, or the local issue of Pearson International Airport. Though there were some responses concerning these issues, the overwhelming concern, 90 per cent of the responses, focused on this government's unfair taxation policy.
My constituents are horrified that after five years of empty Tory rhetoric about tax reform, the most progressive concept this government could come up with is the goods and services tax, a tax that is being called regressive, inflationary and the greatest one-shot tax grab in Canadian history.
At a recent Tory convention in Ottawa, Mr. Wilson told the party faithful that the GST is unpopular but necessary. Well, Mr. Wilson is only half right. The tax is unpopular, but it is not necessary.
A quick look at the history of the Tory record shows this government has failed dismally on its promise to bring about tax reform. For example, Tory tax reform since 1984 has meant that an unmarried individual living at the StatsCan poverty line has had his taxes increased by 38.9 per cent under this government. By contrast, a single individual earning a salary of $60,000 has had only a 6 per cent tax increase. This is Tory tax reform?
Another example is the one-income family with two children who live at the poverty level of $24,000. The Prime Minister and Michael Wilson have increased the tax bite on this family by a whopping 61 per cent.

Once again, by contrast, the family earning $100,000 has had its taxes increased by only 7.7 per cent.
Canadians are learning to say: "If this is the Renaissance take us back to the Dark Ages". The new goods and services tax appears to be the silver lining in a full metal jacket. When the finance minister first introduced the idea he promised that the GST would be a tremendous advantage over the manufacturers' tax because it would be visible to the consumer. Well, more trickery, more treachery awaits. The premiers recognize that this is an ill-conceived administrative nightmare of a tax and they are simply not prepared to participate in the finance minister's folly. This tax has not accomplished any of its intended and promised goals.
The GST will not be visible because, as the minister himself stated, the federal government does not have the legal authority to impose a method of collection on Canadian retailers. Consumers will be left in the dark about tax. Is the price pre-taxed, un-taxed or re-taxed? The only thing consumers will know is that they are over-taxed. This government's vision of tax reform is nothing more than raze and pillage.
It is estimated that the GST will plunder at least $6 billion more from the taxpayers than the old manufacturers' tax. This figure, which was rounded off from the government's own technical paper, flies in the face of the finance minister's other promise that the value-added tax would be revenue neutral. This tax is not neutral. It is acid for most Canadians.
Like this government's other tax measures it is nothing more than a thinly veiled attempt to gouge the average Canadian. Not long ago you may remember the bank robber who wore a transparent plastic bag over his head when he approached a teller. Canadians can see through the finance minister's disguise.
It is distressing to listen to the Prime Minister's glib statements in defence of the proposal over the past few months. He has repeatedly tried to mislead Canadians by saying that a 9 per cent goods and services tax is a major improvement over the manufacturers' 13.5 per cent and that consumers may even see costs go down. I wonder if after receiving so many reports, so many failing grades from everybody, from the Canadian Chamber of Commerce to the National Anti-Poverty Organization, the GST will mean lower prices for Canadians. The Prime
Supply
Minister, like old Ebenezer, will find his conscience after seeing the ghost of elections yet to come.
Let me explain how the new tax will work. Under the current manufacturer's tax, a sofa which costs $500 to produce will be taxed at the rate of 13.5 per cent, or roughly $67, for a total shipping cost of $567. Under the GST any tax that is paid in the transfer of product from producer to producer will be rebated to the manufacturer or retailer with the entire value-added tax placed on the final retail price, which is saved for the consumer, the average Canadian, to pay. So our example of the $500 sofa shipped to the retailer and marked up 100 per cent on the store floor will have the consumer shelling out $1,090. That is $90 in tax compared to the original $67. That is, of course, assuming that the manufacturer will not just alter his original price structure and continue to ship out the sofa at $567.
Perhaps the Prime Minister's mathematics may fool his cheerleaders on the finance committee but it does not seem to have fooled anyone else. If this is the Prime Minister's vision of tax reduction then we can understand the debt doubling under his direction. The minister has countered these complaints by saying that all taxes are unpopular. No one, he says, likes new taxes and so the thousands of ordinary Canadians who have signed petitions written to their MPs and have appeared before the committee do not matter.
If the Prime Minister will not listen, then perhaps he should listen to some of this former allies. He should listen to what business groups have to say about the GST. Groups such as the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and the Canadian Real Estate Board. What more does the minister need?
Mr. Bulloch of the Federation of Independent Business which represents 82,000 small businesses has said- and this has been confirmed by many businesses in my own riding-that Canada will witness an unprecedented number of small business closures. Companies that are already operating on narrow profit margins will be cut to the bone. The hairdresser, the variety store owner, the shoe repairman are all examples of business people who will find themselves absorbing the cost of a new tax in order to remain competitive. This is not to mention the extra cost of the paperwork needed to administer this paper nightmare. The small business will be hurt in other ways as well. The GST will reduce the over-all buying power of Canadians, raise unemployment levels and generally slow economic growth. These combined factors

Madam Speaker, I am all in favour of education. I gladly take up the minister's invitation to meet with him and review the figures. Perhaps we can agree to resume debate after we have done so.
I have one question for the minister. Is this GST or is it the FTA tax?

I listened with interest to the hon. member's presentation. I wonder if she could elaborate on a point. The Conservative government indicates that the reason for this tax is to replace the manufacturers' tax which is a killer of jobs. I think that is the name the Minister of Finance used when he described it, yet it is my recollection that when the Conservatives took office it was at 9 per cent, which is the same level that has been proposed for GST. Over the years it was raised to 10 per cent, 11 per cent, 12 per cent, 13 per cent, and then 13.5 per cent. If the government is serious about saying that this tax is terrible, that it mitigates against our exporters and favours foreigners, that it is a killer of jobs, why would the government increase it four times during its term of office?
I can only conclude that some of the finance minister's economic advisers have perhaps studied in Argentina and their theories should be tested on animals.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to stand in the House today to speak to this motion. I would like to reiterate what the motion is: "That this House condemns the government for its mismanagement of the Canadian economy", and then it cites five aspects of that mismanagement.
I want to point out that this mismanagement is not an accident. It is consistent with the government's political philosophy. It is consistent with the government's vision and it is consistent with the government's overconfidence in the market as the device to solve all problems.
This approach to our economic woes, this vision, this mismanagement, represents what we are now facing in Canada. As my colleague from Sault Ste. Marie said earlier this morning, the government does not like to talk about the free trade agreement any more. We in my party are going to continue to talk about the free trade agreement. The measures that this government is bring-

ing in now are components of that trade deal with the United States. This is what harmonization means.
I will address my comments to just two of those components: first, the changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act. The Canadian Labour Congress last week released startling new figures which demonstrate just how bad the impact of the government's Unemployment Insurance Act will be. While Bill C-21 takes a number of harmful steps, the CLC figures examine only one aspect, and I should be clear about that, that is the increase in the number of weeks of work required to be eligible for benefits.
According to government figures there will be only 30,000 people who would not be able to get enough weeks of work to qualify for benefits. The CLC, however, paid Statistics Canada to produce a study based on the impact of Bill C-21 on people who received benefits in 1988. According to Statistics Canada 128,724 people would not have had enough weeks of work to obtain benefits. This is four times the government's figure.
In British Columbia the government says only 3,000 will be affected. Statistics Canada figures demonstrate that the real figure is 15,845 people. On Vancouver Island where I come from the figures are 3,060 people. This has an economic impact of $15 million lost to my region of the country. When we talk about mismanagement, we also have to talk about the careful manipulation of figures. The government has been withholding this information. It released only some of it in August, four months after tabling the proposal, only because of an access to information request.
The second component of this free trade agreement is the goods and services tax. When any major policy is introduced, it is wise to look at who will benefit and who will suffer. I think Canadians, in spite of a $7 million plus ad campaign, know that they are not going to benefit. It is going to be big business, not small business, that will benefit from this.
It is small business that was talking to the finance committee in droves. I was there when the Chamber of Commerce group came, when the Home Builders Association gave its presentation, and when the construction industry came to give its presentation. They understand

in spite of this $7 million ad campaign that this is not good news. I think, though, that we have to understand that this is a component of the free trade agreement.
My colleague from Edmonton East in a question in the House on Friday alluded to some of the dimensions of the free trade agreement and the goods and services tax as relates to energy. In the free trade debate last year a lot of focus was put on energy. As my colleague from Edmonton East pointed out, the goods and services tax is adding 9 per cent to energy costs, the same energy that we sell to the United States. But the goods and services tax is not included in exports, so the United States purchasers do not have that GST added and will get the energy for 9 per cent less than what Canadians pay for it. These issues are components of a free trade agreement. You can be assured that on this side of the House the free trade agreement is going to be there to haunt this government for many years to come.
Some colleagues of mine have stated that this government is going to be among the most hated of governments come the next election, and we in our party are going to be there to make sure that the people understand that and that we provide an alternative.

speakeroldname: Mr. Michel Champagne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Forestry)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Forestry)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak to this Opposition motion of censure, presented mainly by the Liberals, and I want to read the motion, which says:
That this House condemns the Government for its
mismanagement of the Canadian economy, including:
4) abandonment of Canadian primary producers with resulting undermining of the farming, fishing and forest industries;
Madam Speaker, I find it rather ironic that an Opposition motion, mainly sponsored by the Liberals, should deal with this subject, especially the forestry sector. Let me provide some background. Twenty-nine years ago, in June 1960, the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker, Prime Minister of Canada, rose in this House to propose a bill that would create a department of forestry for the first time in Canada's history. On July 11, 1960, the bill was passed unanimously by the House, on both second and
third reading. Royal assent was given on August 1, and the new department was established on October 1,1960. And it was a Liberal Government, Madam Speaker, that invalidated this major step, that abolished the Department of Forestry so that we now have to go back and repeat the process.
The motion presented by the Liberals condemns the Government for abandoning the forestry industry. I think we should condemn the Opposition for ignoring the forestry sector, especially as far as interest rates are concerned. Remember the period from 1980 to 1984, when interest rates were so high that most people in business had tremendous trouble recovering from the impact and people in the primary sectors such as farming, fisheries and forestry suffered considerable losses and in some cases even went bankrupt.
Madam Speaker, it is indeed ironic that the Liberals should present this kind of motion. If we look at what happened in 1984 when the Progressive Conservative Party came to power and what has happened since then in the forestry sector, I think it is clear that some very important initiatives have been taken.
First of all, when we came to power in 1984, we had promised during the election campaign to appoint a minister of State, and we did, Madam Speaker. Second, when we came to power in 1984, federal provincial relations, or what was left of them, were very troubled. Quebec was no longer on speaking terms with the federal Government. The provinces were no longer on speaking terms with the federal Government, and vice versa, because of the unmitigated arrogance with which the Liberals approached the provinces and the areas under their jurisdiction.
What we have done in the forestry sector since 1984 has been to sign federal-provincial agreements with each province, agreements that represent nearly $1 billion invested over five years, from 1985 to 1990, of which $662 million is federal funding, with the remaining $500 million contributed by the provinces. Madam Speaker, in Quebec, and more specifically in the region I represent-Region 04-the Canada-Quebec Agreement, which, I may add, is worth $300 million, of which $150 million is federal money, has generated nearly $29,279,860, which breaks down as follows: public forests, $19,833,950; private forests, $8,381,530 and $1,064,380 on Indian reserves and federal land.

That is the situation in my riding. Producers in the farming and forestry sectors know that the Progressive Conservative Government has done a great deal for the forestry industry since 1984, and contrary to the motion presented by the Liberals, they realize how conscious we are of their concerns and how anxious we were to reach a compromise with the federal Government that would make it possible for our producers, our businesses, our young people and our business people to invest in a prosperous industry, in one of the activity sectors that generates the most jobs in Quebec, 1 out of 17, and is also very important in terms of economic spinoffs.
Madam Speaker, in the riding of Champlain, the Canada-Quebec Agreement on forestry development has provided nearly $17,433,860 in funding, which breaks down as follows: $14,539,430 for public forests and $1,830,006 for private forests. Plus $1,064,380 for Indian reserves and other federal land. Madam Speaker, this proves without a doubt there is no hint of partisanship here since we are dealing with a provincial-liberal government that when it was necessary to reach a consensus with the provinces and provide for the recovery of an economic sector that had been abandoned by the Liberals, this federal Government was able to find ways to reach that consensus.
If I may refresh the memory of the Liberals with respect to forestry, we established the Canadian Council of Forestry Ministers in 1985. We developed a national forestry strategy in 1987. And finally, as I said earlier, we are now setting up the legislative committee for Bill C-29, a proposal to establish a full-fledged department of forestry. In fact, both Opposition parties support us on a proposal, once implemented in 1960 and later demolished by the Liberals.
The goods and services tax is a vital part of the Government's long-term strategy for establishing a viable economic policy. Once the goods and services tax is in place, the federal tax system will be more progressive, and low-income Canadians will be better off. This will be achieved thanks to a new refundable credit. The credit will be paid quarterly, before the goods and services are purchased by households.
Supply
Implementation of the goods and services tax should have the following impact on the forestry sector: production costs will drop, since the new tax will not apply to goods required in the manufacturing process, thus making our producers more competitive on domestic and foreign markets. Wood products for export will not be taxed, thus making them more competitive on international markets. Furthermore, as in other sectors, manufacturers of wood products will be able to claim input tax credits on goods and services acquired for use in manufacturing their products. Indeed, the goods and services tax will encourage a more effective use of our economy's resources, promote exports and make Canadian products more competitive, both on Canadian and foreign markets. It will also encourage new investment, while an increase in the number of jobs in the forestry sector is expected.
Removal of the manufacturer's tax will strengthen the position of Canadian products, including wood products, on Canadian and international markets. The result will be increased productivity and more jobs for Canadians. And finally, Madam Speaker, increased productivity, improved competition and lower capital costs will affect the growth of investment and strengthen foreign trade. These factors will increase production and employment from the first year the goods and services tax takes effect. We also expect that the goods and services tax, by replacing the present manufacturers' sales tax, will result in lower industrial and commercial construction costs, which should increase the demand for this type of construction. Note that this kind of construction is exempt from the GST because the products used are not at the end of the consumption chain. Note that the lumber and paneling used in non-residential construction is very important for the lumber industry. About half of these products are for the domestic market and used for non-residential construction. This is especially important for Quebec and Ontario which are much more dependent on the Canadian market than are the other regions of the country are.
We also expect lower costs for writing and wrapping paper, for cardboard not used for food packaging and for tissue and toilet paper. The tax on these products is now 13.5 per cent at the manufacturer's level, but it will be 9 per cent with the GST. Tax reform will thus benefit

Supply
producers and consumers of these products. Note that these products have a high added value compared to most other forest products.
Also, Madam Speaker, the GST or goods and services tax reform will cancel any sales tax now imposed on goods used in manufacturing. Let us mention motor fuel, vehicles, computers, office furniture, services, telecommunications. At present, taxes on these products are invisible in the selling price and reduce the efficiency of investment.
Madam Speaker, in conclusion, because I know that my time is running out, I would like to say to the whole House that the goods and services tax will have a positive effect on employment and job creation, especially in the forestry sector, Madam Speaker.
I would like to remind the Opposition that the Government's record in recent years is positive because it has given this industry its rightful place in Canadian industry and the Canadian economy, namely first place.

Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member who just spoke was talking about forestry policy, but I have the impression he was trying to lose us in a thicket of figures and facts. And I think he was also being overly optimistic when he said that the new tax, the GST, was going to improve things. That is not how we see it, especially since 79 per cent of Canadians are not happy with the way you are managing public funds, and why should they be?
However, what is really at issue in this debate is not forestry policy. I can inform the Hon. Member that the provinces have their own forestry policies and have had them for many years. If you intend to enter into agreements with the provinces, as you propose to do with this new tax, we will really be up the creek.
Basically, the motion says that the new goods and services tax will be a menace because, first of all, it will lead to inflation across the board and is regressive, inequitable and invisible. Of course it is!
What we must consider with this goods and services tax is that the Government's only strategy in this instance is
that it does not want to deal with the real problem in this country, which is that we need a complete tax reform, from A to Z.
All the observers and tax experts tell us that every year it is getting more and more difficult and complex for the average Canadian to complete his income tax return, especially when he sees his taxes going up every year. We don't have to quote figures all day long to realize there is something wrong with the tax system in this country. We have statistics indicating that thousands of Canadians don't pay income tax, that Canadian companies don't pay income tax, that all kinds of companies have managed to defer income tax payments for years, which of course has an impact on the federal Government's revenues.

This tax on goods and services is the greatest cover-up I think we will have ever seen in the House of Commons. The basic problem that we have here is that the whole tax system is out of control. You do not have to have an economics degree from any university to realize that the tax system is the most detrimental thing against the middle class that we have seen in the last 25 years.
All that you have to do is take a look at the last 25 years to 30 years, especially after the Carter commission that was unfortunately not published, to see that the tax system even then needed an overhaul. Here we are coming along with an additional proposed tax of 9 per cent. It is obvious that 79 per cent of the people of this country feel that it is unjust and that it is going to create more difficulties for the average Canadian.
The basic problem that we have to face is to admit, to begin with, that our tax system needs to be completely overhauled. I admit I have been influenced by a book called Behind Closed Doors which was written in conjunction with the best tax expert in this country who indicated that the so-called tax loopholes were because of nothing but lobbyists in this country.

Mr. Speaker, five weeks ago I and a committee of Liberals from RE.I. took up the Tory challenge of coming up with alternatives to the defence department closing of military bases as a means of satisfying the finance minister's deficit cutting requirements.
After much research and study we proposed that one of the military bases, Summerside, be used to establish a UN international peacekeeping training centre. Funding would come primarily from the UN and participating nations, and while Canadian government contributions to the camp would drop from $40 million to about $10 million, there would be little drop in personnel.
The proposal was received with great acclaim by many experts in the arms control and disarmament community. That is not surprising because there are many up sides. Canada would be able to apply and share its internationally recognized expertise and experience in peacekeeping. It would be afforded a leadership role in an increasingly important aspect of external affairs, and foreign capital would replace the funds from DND and breathe life into the local economy.
I urge the Minister of National Defence to take a serious and hard look at our alternative and he can call on our committee for help.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to bring to the attention of the House the fact that today is the start of Family Week in Canada. As we enter the 1990s the definition of family is changing. The number of children being raised in one parent families and the number of children living in poverty are on the rise. There are 1.2 million Canadian children living in poverty. Internationally, 40,000 children die each day because of the poor economic conditions in which they live.
Children are poor because their parents are poor and family benefits are being eroded by this Tory government. The claw-back of family allowances, destruction of UI, the failure to provide national child care strategy, the lack of affordable housing, and the introduction of the goods and services tax makes the job of parenting more and more impossible for Canadian families.
While we celebrate the week of the family we must remember that much more needs to be done to support families in Canada and throughout the world. It is a sobering thought to recognize that in the one minute I have been given to make this statement, 27 children around the world have died from poverty.

Mr. Speaker, last Saturday night the Red Deer Chamber of Commerce honoured David and Linda Hueppelsheuser as farm family of the year, and Wayne Lalor for his dedicated service to youth and sports programs.
They also paid tribute to the person chosen as citizen of the year, a man who has dedicated a lifetime of service to the community of Red Deer. In the words of the

presenter, even in his political position, he constantly went far beyond the normal expectations to help his fellow citizens.
I am sure you will be pleased to know that Red Deer has honoured as its citizen of the year a former colleague, Mr. Gordon Towers, Mr. Speaker. In his acceptance speech for the award, a surprised Mr. Towers accepted humbly, quoting Tennyson, saying that he had "received much from others as each of us is a part of all we have met". He went on to say that he is not yet finished and he still has work to do. It is obvious, Mr. Speaker, that he did not intend to let his service stop when he left this place and Red Deer will reap the benefits of that service.

Mr. Speaker, the recent decision by the United States International Trade Commission to impose a 3.6 cents per pound, countervail duty on Canadian fresh chilled and frozen pork is one of the best examples of the failure of the free trade deal to protect our farmers from the whims of U.S. farm lobby groups.
The free trade deal was going to provide certainty instead of uncertainty in the face of U.S. trade protection as we were told by the Prime Minister. The only certainty Canadians can expect out of this government and this trade deal is more challenges to our food security and to our farmers and their farms.
This countervail duty is sure to affect farm gate prices and cost millions to Canadian farmers. Farmers can hardly afford to stay in business with the way things are going. U.S. legislators made it clear last fall after the Congress passed the free trade deal that they had no intention of guaranteeing access to the U.S. market for Canadian pork when they amended the omnibus trade bill.
It is high time the government went back to the drawing board before its ineffective trade policies spell certain doom for Canadian farmers.

Mr. Speaker, today marks the second annual Development Day, a day designated by the federal government to shed light on international development issues and to reflect upon what we can do to better the living conditions in the Third World.
Canadians are justifiably proud of our record as a caring and as a compassionate people. Our record in the field of international development is unrivalled. In the developing world the maple leaf is a symbol of hope and co-operation.
Unfortunately, this record is in jeopardy. Since the April budget the over-riding thought has been cutbacks. Instead of helping people to help themselves, the development community is struggling to cope with far fewer resources. Multilateral food aid was cut by $32 million, bilateral food aid was cut by $24.4 million, our contribution to international institution by $56.5 million and humanitarian assistance by $4.5 million. The list goes on to total over $360 million in cuts with many more on the way next year.
Development Day is the day for all Canadians to reflect on our role in the developing world. More importantly, it is also a day to send a clear message to the government that the time has come to restore funding for development assistance.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the European Economic Community consists of 320 million people in 12 sovereign nations and languages who in this century alone were at war twice, killing millions of people. Yet they have fewer barriers to trade and other differences than we do here in Canada. In spite of a GST tax of up to 28 per cent they are buying

stereos, cars and houses in record numbers. The reason is that the GST is the most equitable and fair tax. By 1992, they will have an economic and social union which will make Canada look like 10 separate and feuding nations.
We are clearly wasting time in Canada over Meech Lake and other petty differences. Meech Lake should have been passed months ago, and we should already have dealt with women's issues, native issues, fisheries and Senate reform. I call upon the opposition parties to start thinking of Canada as a whole rather than always being concerned about the separate, narrow, selfish interests of special groups.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to take a moment of this House to remember a distinguished Manitoban and a former parliamentarian who just recently passed away. Trying to recount all the contributions of Mark Smerchanski, who served in this House from 1968 to 1972, is a difficult task for he was a man of many talents and interests who provided remarkable public service.
A geological engineer by training, he was one of the pioneers in opening up Canada's north to mineral exploration. He was later a professor of engineering and a builder of new techniques in that area.
As a member of the provincial legislature for Burrows and in this House as the member for Provencher, he won the respect and praise of his constituents and was certainly a strong voice for western Canada.
Mark Smerchanski will also be remembered for his major contributions to the Ukrainian-Canadian community. He was instrumental in establishing the Department of Slavic Studies at the University of Manitoba and perhaps took greatest pride in his accomplishment as the founder of the Holy Family Nursing Home in Winnipeg. Mark Smerchanski is survived by his wife Pat and three daughters, Joan, Rhonda and Patricia.
I am sure the House will join me in wanting to send our condolences to his family and thanks to Mark Smerchanski for a life of service to his country.
Hear, hear!

of passengers despite inconvenient schedules, bad service and appalling management. Rather than ending over 100 years of service, the government should upgrade the dayliner in the interests of tourism, community pride, the environment and national unity.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased today to lend my wholehearted support to National Family Week which starts today and runs through to October 8. This government provides support to the Canadian family in many broad and diverse ways. We run programs for seniors and the disabled. We administer comprehensive income support networks. We are working on a national strategy to reduce violence in the family. Our child care initiatives fund is supporting quality child care services across Canada.
National Family Week asks us to be more sensitive to the needs of our families and to celebrate the strength, the joy, and the vitality of the Canadian family.
I would like to ask all members of the House to join me in support of National Family Week and to enjoy the riches our family lives offer each of us.

Mr. Speaker, on Friday, September 29, the Minister of National Health and Welfare and I toured three day care centres in the city of North York and met with representatives of the North York Interagency Council. We visited a workplace infant and toddler centre with rent and building costs paid for by the city. This centre took six months to fill as a result of the freeze on subsidies caused by the lack of provincial funding. As a result, only 19 of 58 spaces are available to low income families.
We visited a day care centre in a high school designed to keep teen mothers in school. This centre, which is subsidized and assisted by the board of education, had empty spaces for part of last year due to a lack of subsidies. We visited a neighbourhood centre, also in a public school, where full fee-paying parents were subsidizing low income parents because of the lack of adequate subsidies for low income families. As a result, spaces for parents needing subsidy have been limited. Eight-five per cent of the families needing subsidy are single parent families. Day care subsidy help families to help themselves.
As part of National Family Week, I strongly urge the minister to bring forward a child care program which will ensure that low income families have access to day care and will provide disadvantaged children with the benefits of early literacy, good nutrition and good child care.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday's unbelievable pronouncement by the Minister of Housing that affordable housing is not a national priority in Canada is truly irresponsible as numerous Canadians for a variety of reasons cannot afford to buy a home at all.
Do those living on the streets in cities across Canada find affordable housing not a priority? Do single mothers looking for reasonable accommodation find that affordable housing is not a priority? Do the many families in major centres across this nation who cannot begin to afford a new home because of the skyrocketing prices also find that affordable housing is not a priority?
What belies the statements made by the minister is that he was, before becoming a cabinet minister, a mayor who fought for such issues. He was an outspoken critic of the Conservative government's housing policy right here in the House of Commons. His comments do little to help those in need of basic shelter and are a rebuke of their pleas for action.
I suggest that the minister consult with those he purportedly serves and take concrete measures to house the many Canadians in need. Affordable housing is a national issue. What we need is a minister who recognizes that fact.

Mr. Speaker, almost a year has passed since the last election when the Prime Minister declared that social programs were a sacred trust. However, the government has begun a process of clawing back the safety net and has embarked on an initiative that will severely affect lower and middle-income Canadians.
The Conservative government is blindly committed to a new tax to replace the manufacturers' retail sales tax which would be placed on almost every good and service. One week ago I held a meeting in my riding of Hamilton West on the subject of the proposed tax. Three hundred and fifty people filled the room and not one person was in favour of the government's plan. So far over 5,000
October 2, 1989

signatures have been collected from constituents opposing the tax.
As one of my constituents put it, when a family buys a new home it takes on a deficit. When they buy a new car, it takes on a deficit. What the Minister of Finance is telling Canadians is that they must now increase their deficit to reduce his. And happen it will, as the government proclaims its tax as fact in newspaper ads, circumventing my privileges as the elected representative for the constituents of Hamilton West who say enough is enough.

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Prime Minister and concerns the moral legitimacy of this government.
During the last election the Prime Minister promised a child care program, promised a revenue neutral national sales tax, promised continued universality of social programs, and continued support for VIA Rail. After the election the Prime Minister terminated the child care program, delivered another massive tax increase, destroyed universality of social programs and is now in the business of gutting VIA Rail.
Given that Canadians have no opportunity to pass electoral judgment on this massive fraud for another three years, will the Prime Minister agree today to withhold implementation of the planned route eliminations of VIA Rail and the planned 2,900 lay-offs of VIA employees until public hearings are held across this country on this very important matter?

Mr. Speaker, it is astounding for the House and the country to hear a Liberal rise in this House and talk about moral legitimacy. That is a contradiction in terms. The fact of the matter is that this House passed a child care program which was killed by his Liberal friends in the Senate.
We have a mandate from the people of Canada to deal with matters which are not necessarily popular, but which are right for Canada. Some of these mean reversing some attitudes and some trends of the past, not all of
Oral Questions
them pleasant and not all of them easy. We are not going to do them because they are popular; we are going to do them because they are right for Canada.

Mr. Speaker, according to Webster's Dictionary the word "probity", which used to be a favourite of the Prime Minister's, means upright, upstanding, forthright and honest. It is no wonder he never uses the word anymore.
It staggers the mind to realize that while every other nation in the western world prepares to meet the year 2000 with efficient, environmentally clean, high speed rail passenger service, Canada and Canada alone pursues a policy of increasing reliance on already congested highways and skyways.
I ask the Prime Minister whether or not he will make available all environmental impact studies carried out in preparation for this decision to terminate VIA Rail. In fact I ask whether or not he will give the House, and through the House the people of Canada, an assurance that such environmental impact studies have been carried out pursuant to the government's recently announced policy of doing just that.

Mr. Speaker, I have always said to the House and outside the House that when the decision is known I will provide all necessary documents so that Canadians will understand. It will be the best decision we can make.

Mr. Speaker, neither the Prime Minister nor the Minister of Transport have been prepared to tell Canadians that they will have a right to be heard on the decision, which was never discussed or announced in advance of the election last November.
I put my question to the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Transport. Given that we cannot receive an answer in the House, an assurance of public hearings on this important question from either the Prime Minister or the Minister of Transport, will the chairman of the Standing Committee of Transport refer this important question to the Commons transport committee immediately?

Mr. Speaker, the question was to the chairman of the committee and all I can tell my hon. colleague is that the

Oral Questions
transport committee is meeting tomorrow morning at 9.30 to discuss that very thing.

Mr. Speaker, I am astounded today to hear the Prime Minister say that savaging VIA Rail is the proper thing to do, but my question is for the Minister of Transport.
According to the multiplier factor used by VIA Rail to gauge job losses, the 2,900 job cuts projected to be announced on Wednesday will grow to 10,200 jobs as the effects mushroom through the economy. The minister knows it because he received these figures months ago from VIA Rail.
Will the minister give us a clear and unequivocal answer, for the first time on this issue, as to why he has kept this vital information from the Canadian public and from the House of Commons?
Mr. Speaker, of course we always release good information to Canadians. Normally, though, it is not based on leaked documents.
Mr. Speaker, I rode VIA Rail this weekend to talk particularly to the employees of VIA Rail. They all know that over half the routes will be cut and 2,980 employees will be fired.
New rider.

Perhaps the hon. gentleman over there should take a turn and ride VIA Rail also, so that he knows of which he speaks.
Another 10,000 Canadian jobs will be directly affected. They all expect this to be announced on Wednesday just before Thanksgiving, and the lay-offs to take place just after Christmas on January 15. All Canadians have the right to know why the minister is doing this to VIA Rail. The minister is duty bound to explain why he is eliminating passenger rail service in Canada. Will the minister appear before the transport committee to explain to the committee and, in fact, to all Canadians why he is doing this to passenger rail service in this country?

Mr. Speaker, that is pretty obvious. Last spring, I appeared twice before the Transport Commitee. I answered all kinds of questions at the time the Hon. Member was there and the vast majority
of the questions were about VIA Rail. I answered the questions, and, at the time, I felt that this was one way of consulting. However, Mr. Speaker, I still feel I cannot give the Hon. Member the answers he wants, because they are not the kind of answers I will give, first of all, but-
The announcement on Wednesday!

He says: The announcement on Wednesday! I have yet to announce when the announcement will be made and so far I have given no indication. Announcements will be made at the appropriate time, as I said earlier, and will be based on valid documents. I just hope the Hon. Member will take VIA Rail more often than he must have done when he was a member of the task force on transport.

Mr. Speaker, obviously, the minister does not know when it will be because he has not found a place in Montreal that will hold 1,500 people for the meeting on Wednesday.
My question is to the Prime Minister. On Friday, the Minister of Transport said, "Normally, when the cost is over the revenue there is a problem". This government has repeatedly promised to buy modem trains for VIA Rail instead of just throwing away hundreds of millions of dollars by maintaining obsolete 35 year old trains resulting in high costs and a waste of taxpayers' money.
Clearly, the Minister of Transport has failed to live up to his responsibilities and that responsibility must now fall on the Prime Minister. When will he act to protect Canadians who use VIA because it is affordable, safe, accessible, environmentally friendly and convenient?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to correct something that my friend said about VIA Rail.
Over the last 10 years the former government and ourselves have put more than $5.4 billion into VIA Rail. Our own government has put more than $.5 billion into the equipment alone. He says that we have not put money into it.
Last week my friend talked a lot about ridership. For the first six months of 1989, the increase in the number of passengers was 2.7 per cent. I would like to be able to manage a corporation with that kind of figure. I would
October 2, 1989

have to know exactly what is the cost; but my friend never gave the costs of the operations of VIA Rail.

Mr. Speaker, it is nice to know that the minister has confirmed the information I gave the House on Friday. I have another supplementary to the Prime Minister.
Last week we heard that bus companies are predicting significant fare increases as soon as VIA Rail is cut. Today, we learned that airline fares are about to go up by hundreds of dollars per ticket.
Will the Prime Minister acknowledge that his government's policies of deregulation and the destruction of VIA Rail are an attack on consumers in all regions of this country. Will he act to protect these consumers by cancelling plans for the elimination of VIA services across this country?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw your attention to a letter I received from the Canadian Bus Association, in which the association's director general says the following:

"I am writing to you to state in clear terms that the telephone interview conducted on September 27 did not contain any reference to the prospect of the bus industry increasing price simply because VIA Rail services are changed".
I believe it is very clear. Once again, we have to tell the truth. We have to use real documents as I am doing here this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, since according to the Minister of Transport, it is very hard to know who is responsible for what in this Cabinet, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Under the proposed changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act, nearly 5,000 people in Montreal will no longer be eligible for benefits. Over 8,000 people depend either directly or indirectly on VIA Rail for their employment in this city. We see the same scenario in Halifax, Winnipeg and elsewhere in this country. Does the Prime Minister intend to take the necessary measures to protect Cana-

dians who may be out of a job and without any financial support?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think that my friend, the Minister of Transport, has been forthcoming about what the government is looking at in connection with VIA Rail. Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. It concerns the devastating effect on the tourism industry of the proposed GST.
In the Atlantic region alone over $2 billion are infused into the local economy because of tourism. In Nova Scotia, 1.6 million tourists leave over $760 million in the local economy.
The effect of the proposed GST will be to send many of these tourists who are seeking a seaside holiday stateside. That is where they will be leaving their money. What measures will this government take to protect this industry which is so vital to a region that has already been battered half to death by this Government's economic policies?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the first thing we are doing is we are exempting foreign tourists from the GST on products they buy in Canada, as well as accommodation that they buy in Canada. They will not be taxed, either, on their plane flights into the country.
I will tell the hon. member something else. We have worked hard with the tourism industry to make sure that it has a competitive advantage with other countries. France, Britain, Germany, for example, have tax programs just like we have. We are going to have a GST. Their tourism has increased by almost 100 per cent over the last four years. Let us make sure that our industry is

October 2, 1989

helped and not pulled down by exaggerations, by defective attacks like this.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, that is a tremendous amount of gall. Some 74 per cent of the travelling public that go into Atlantic Canada are Canadians. What the minister has just said is that Americans will be given preferential treatment over Canadians under this government's economic policy.
My question is again for the Minister of Finance. Given that your government has gutted regional development programs, has mismanaged the fisheries into a state of complete collapse and probably Wednesday or Thursday of this week is prepared to drive the last spike into the heart of the travelling rail public in Atlantic Canada, will you finally not now say that the GST-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must ask hon. members to put their questions through the Chair.
Will the minister now not see that his GST proposal is fatally flawed and withdraw it immediately? Or, is he hell-bent in shutting down yet another industry in Atlantic Canada? That is the question.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, the content of the member's question with a large amount of exaggeration on the various things related to the gutting of regional development is nonsense. This government has maintained a veiy high level of regional development spending, 50 per cent higher than it was in previous years. The hon. member knows that.
The hon. member also knows that there has been no mismanagement whatsoever of the fisheries industry in Atlantic Canada. In fact we have been working very hard with the industry and with our representations to people in other countries to ensure that we maintain a healthy fisheries industry in Canada.
The hon. member would do his region a good deal more credit and a give a good deal more assistance if he would avoid the exaggerations and start talking facts.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. The 9 per cent goods and services tax proposal discriminates against the residents of the northern regions of Canada. Because our cost of living in the north is the highest in the country, each northerner will pay more of this unfair tax. None of the public documents of the proposed GST have assessed the impact of this tax on northerners.
My question for the minister is this: Why was the north omitted from the government's technical paper? Has the government done any background studies on the impact of this tax on the north? If so, will the minister release these studies to northerners?

Mr. Speaker, I should draw to the member's attention that we have done a good deal of work on the impact of the tax on the north. If the hon. member did not just isolate one element but looked at the over-all impact of the tax on the economy of the north, I could tell him that the impact on the north is about the same as the national average. In other words, it will improve the economic fortunes of the north by about 1.5 per cent. That is equivalent to what the national average is.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I wish to draw to the attention of members the presence in the gallery of Mr. Anders Bjorck, President of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe.
Hear, hear!

speechtext: The hon. member for Churchill.
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. Given that today the minister is aware that the-

Mr. Speaker, it is quite clear that we did not get an answer from the Minister of Finance so I my supplementary to him.
October 2, 1989

It is quite obvious that the government did not give any consideration to the north even though the effects will be devastating. I would like to know if the minister will commit to determining the impact of the tax on tourism, on inflation, on the cost of transportation, on construction, on housing, and justify why northerners should pay a much higher dollar value for the tax on the same item than in the south.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, in fact I did give her colleague an answer, and I got quite a precise answer.
The answer is that if you take into account all aspects of the tax-not just one or two or three different aspects of the tax but all aspects of the tax-and the impact of that on the economy of the north, the answer that I gave her colleague and the answer that I will give her is that there is a positive impact on the region of the north. The amount is about a 1.5 per cent increase, which is about the same as the national average.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister has had notice of this question now.
Given the fact that the fish workers in Nova Scotia in attempting to save their jobs are stopping the export of raw fish from that province, what is the minister going to do to live up to his responsibility and keep jobs in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member would know that fish harvested in Canadian waters on both of our coasts and in the central areas as well leave Canada in various forms, including fresh fish which goes into many markets where it commands a higher price than processed fish.
We believe that we should gain maximum employment advantage from our raw materials, but a recent ruling by the GATT makes it quite clear that Canada cannot restrict the export of unprocessed fish to certain markets which demand it. In fact, many fishing companies and many fishermen benefit by this practice. Nonetheless, we encourage maximum processing and maximum opportunity being extracted from the resource in Canada.
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, that is simply not good enough. Since July of this year over 8 million pounds of B.C. raw salmon have gone to the United States. Last year, over 80 million pounds of raw fish went from Nova Scotia to the United States. The thing is that the minister has not taken his responsibility. He has done nothing to save those jobs. When is he going to start acting?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member would know or should know that the Pacific coast fishing industry, which he mentions, has enjoyed its most abundant year in history in the quantity of fish harvested and the amount of employment provided to Canadian workers. That is a fact.
Were it not for certain problems with exchange rates and international fish prices, we would have far more employment in Atlantic Canada. Nonetheless, we have a very healthy fishery in this country, and the member knows that.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport.
Nearly 700,000 litres of fuel were spilled in a derailment that occurred in Press, Abitibi around 1981. Today, eight years later, some of that fuel is coming back to the surface.
My question is as follows: Could the Minister assure us that Canadian National will install a permanent reservoir immediately, before next winter, to separate the oil from the water and to recover the petroleum spilled?
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to tell my colleague from Abitibi that the reservoir in question should indeed be installed by next winter-that is, within a few weeks.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Farmers in Elk Island want to know more about the GST. How long will they wait for the input tax rebate-60 days, 90 days, six

October 2, 1989
Oral Questions
months? Our farmers are important. How long will they have to wait?

Mr. Speaker, the position of the farmers in the goods and services tax proposal is, I think, quite a good one. Because food is not taxed, and because the products that these individuals sell is tax-free, they will receive a full credit on all these business inputs.
The credit will come not in the length of time that the hon. member has suggested but 21 days after they request the credit. If they do not receive it after 21 days they will receive full interest, so they will get their cash flow well looked after during this period of time, and very quickly.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question as well for my good friend the Minister of Fisheries fresh from his, if I may say so, pitiful performance at the NAFO talks a couple of weeks ago. In my riding of Burin-St. George's alone, 16,000 plant workers and fishermen are looking down the barrel of permanent unemployment, thanks to the minister's bungling of the fisheries crisis.
I want to ask him this question: Has he had discussions with National Sea and with Fish Products International about options to ensure that those plant workers and fishermen are able to keep their jobs? Also, can he assure us that the Canada-U.S. free trade provisions will not prevent the minister and the government from honouring its obligation under the 1983 fisheries restructuring agreement to keep certain fish plants open?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member knows full well that he does no service to his constituents by exaggerating and spreading fear that 16,000 workers, as he characterized it, will be without work.
We have certain difficulties in the fishery this year resulting from a number of factors, some of which involve international supply and demand and exchange rates because our fish products from Atlantic Canada are largely exported.
The hon. member knows that a special committee of cabinet on which several of my colleagues and I participate is looking into all facets of this problem. The hon. member also knows that in most respects fishermen in Atlantic Canada are enjoying a year which is prosperous and adequate for their needs in many parts of Atlantic Canada but not as abundant as it has been in the last three or four years in relative comparison.
Mr. Speaker, they will be delighted to hear that they are enjoying it because they did not know that. Now cut out the baloney, Tom; cut out the bombast.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member will put his question.

Mr. Speaker, last spring the Secretary of State for External Affairs was appointed to head up a fish committee. We have not heard from him since.
I ask the minister this question: Can he now finally tell the House what specific plans he has to bring in an assistance package to keep those fishermen and plant workers working, even if we have to share the work until such time as the fish stocks rebound?

Mr. Speaker, as I have indicated already, the special committee continues its deliberations. When the quotas are set for next year, 1990, we will have a far greater indication of the availability of supply to the industry, and at the same time any measures which might be required supplementary to those available from existing programs will be announced, if required, at that time.

Mr. Speaker, in the spring of 1987 in a speech to the University of Waterloo the Prime Minister said the following and I quote:
We know that foreign controlled subsidiaries conduct less R and D than Canadian controlled companies.
And he went on to note that:
The strategic development of Canada depends upon information technologies, industrial materials and biotechnology.
In light of the Prime Minister's own statements in that speech, I want to ask him this questions: Why is the government standing idly by while the acknowledged
October 2, 1989

flagship of Canada's biotechnology industry, Connaught Labs, is being subject to a foreign takeover?
Will the Prime Minister outline today what steps the government intends to take under the authority of the Investment Canada Act to stop the takeover of Connaught and to ensure that Canada has a Canadian owned centre for biotechnology research?
