speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member knows, under the Investment Canada Act full authority is there to ensure that any foreign takeovers, including this one, are to the net benefit of Canada. That examination is under way.

Mr. Speaker, let me ask the minister, then, a specific question.
As he knows, under section 15 of that act the government has the right to stop any takeover that affects cultural heritage and national identity.
Let me ask this question of the Minister. Does the Minister agree that Connaught Labs, the home base of Banting and Best, is part of Canada's national identity? As a result, will he put on notice today that this government intends to use section 15 to stop the takeover of Connaught Labs and keep it under Canadian ownership?

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will certainly give commitment to the House that the Investment Canada Act will be followed. After the proper kind of examination which is called for under the act a decision will be taken. The hon. member seems to be suggesting we should take a decision now and do the analysis later.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of the Environment. On January 31, the Minister promised Canadians: "Where environmental considerations will conflict with economic ones the environment will prevail".
Canadians know that the GST fails to recognize the difference between environmentally friendly and polluting products. Canadians know that the cuts to VIA Rail will force the travelling public to depend more on
Oral Questions
polluting forms of transportation. Bad environmental policies are being forced on Canada by the Minister of Finance.
Will the Minister today show some leadership and announce that he is going to subject the GST to a full environmental impact assessment?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government's existing environmental assessment directives involve several aspects. But the aspect on budgeting in particular does not fit in at all with already existing mechanisms.
That is why we are preparing legislation for the House to give the country a flexible, comprehensive, professional mechanism to deal with any eventuality.
As for the GST in particular, Mr. Speaker, I believe that a measure that will enable Canada to take its rightful place on international markets so that we can create jobs here and improve the sales of Canadian products abroad will put the country's economy on a sound footing to deal with the great environmental challenge.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister obviously does not know that the tax system is one of the most effective places, not least effective places, to assist in promoting environmentally friendly products.
My supplementary is to the Prime Minister who, on October 15,1988 said: "We are prepared to subject every federal undertaking to a full environmental impact study".
Last week the Secretary General of the Brundtland commission noted: "Canada is a country noted for leading with rhetoric and following others with action".
Will the Prime Minister live up to his promise and subject the GST to his own promise and to his own words from last year?

Mr. Speaker, I have not seen the comment from the Secretary of the Brundtland commission, but I have seen comments from Prime Minister Brundtland herself who chaired the commission. She said that Canada's record led the industrialized world. It should be viewed by all

Oral Questions
Canadians with pride in regard to what we have done in the environment.
Hear, hear!

With regard to the matters raised in respect of taxation and others, the Minister of the Environment has responded fully about his intention to bring forward what I believe will be an important and landmark piece of legislation as it affects the environment. I hope my hon. friend and members of the Liberal Party who profess to support the environment will at that point in time rise and give it the enthusiastic support of which they are capable.

Mr. Speaker, my question this day, Development Day, is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs in the absence of the Minister for External Relations.
As demonstrated in the April budget under cuts to overseas development assistance, this government has cast a blind eye to the world's poor and sanctimoniously throws them but scraps from our table. Dozens of Canadian non-governmental organization projects have had to be cancelled. Millions of the world's poorest will suffer because of these foreign aid cuts. The poor do not understand our minister's double talk about quality versus quantity of assistance. They do understand the fine line between life and death.
Will the government not review its foreign aid priorities and return to Canadian NGOs the funds chopped in the April budget enabling them to meet their grass roots assistance projects budgets?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada's program of delivery of aid to the poorest is one of the most effective in the world. We intend to keep it one of the most effective in the world.
Now there were budget cuts in the last budget. I would have preferred, as everyone in this government would have preferred, to have inherited an economy that was strong enough and that was free enough of deficits that we would not have had to engage in the kind of major
cuts that we have had to engage in across the board. But that was not the situation we inherited.
We came into office after a period of reckless spending by the Liberal Party and government. We have to take account of that for several reasons, including the capacity of this country to maintain the kind of economic growth that will allow us to deliver effective aid in the world including particularly to the poor.

I challenge the minister to tell that to the thousands of the world's poor, the rickshaw drivers in Bangladesh, the purse sellers in Ivory Coast, the malnourished children in Lima, Peru.
My supplementary is to the same minister. It is interesting that the budgets directed to the poorest individuals at the grass root level are cut, yet CIDA's own budgets for administrative costs and publicity have risen by $114 million.
Our foreign aid target is gone. Which is the greater need, the need of this minister and the government to promote itself and its structure or the needs of the poor?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Without any doubt and without any argument, the greater need is the need of the poor. That is why the policies of this government have been directed so consistently and so effectively toward helping the poorest in the world.
I suppose what we will hear next from the hon. member is a suggestion that we should not be proceeding with the decentralization in CIDA that was proposed unanimously by a committee of this House.
It was proposed for the very reason of ensuring that we are making our policy based upon the needs of the poor in the regions where Canada is trying to contribute to development assistance and not in relation to the whims or the partisan comments of the day that might arise here in Ottawa.
Mr. Speaker, the former Prime Minister is disgracing himself with an answer like that.

police are not using it. Is the Minister prepared today, instead of keeping all the confiscated profits of crime in Ottawa, to turn them all over to the government or police force that did the work to confiscate them?

Hear, hear!

Oral Questions INDIAN AFFAIRS

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Indian Affairs I would like to direct my question to the Prime Minister as well.
Today, 1,200 elementary school children of the Six Nations near Brantford have entered the second month of their boycott of Department of Indian Affairs schools because the schools have failed to meet fire code standards, basic safety standards, health standards with respect to water, to drainage and to washroom facilities, and asbestos content.
A study by the Department of Indian Affairs in 1985 condemned four schools and proposed substantial repairs to the two remaining schools and replacement of the condemned facilities. This became a promise of the Department of Indian Affairs. After four years, Six Nations children have been forced to go to school in condemned schools that are unhealthy and renovations to only one of the remaining schools has been completed.
What will the government do to keep its promise to replace the condemned Six Nations schools and to completely renovate the remaining schools so that Six Nations children can go to school under the same safe, healthful, decent conditions as non-Indian children in this country?

speakeroldname: Mrs. Dorothy Dobbie (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to inform the hon. gentleman that the department is fully aware of the situation, that it has it well in hand, and that the situation is being addressed.
The hon. member might be interested to know that the students are being well taken care of and that then-long-term objective will be met over time.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary questions is for the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
Does that parliamentary secretary consider it adequate for kids to be taught at home because government controlled Department of Indian Affairs schools are unsafe, are infested with rats, with snakes, have floors

and ceilings and walls that are infested with asbestos? Would she like to see her children go to school under these conditions? Is that what she means by taken well in had?
I would ask the parliamentary secretary: When are those schools going to be upgraded to the standards enjoyed by the rest of Canadians?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, once again the hon. member exaggerates the circumstances. The students are being looked after. We are aware that there are problems with the conditions of the school but temporary measures have been taken to ensure that those students are properly housed in the mean time.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the part-time Minister of Agriculture.
Over the past few months we have seen the U.S. retaliate against our dairy industry, our pork industry and our steel industry. Now we hear the American wheat growers are going to ask for a countervail. All this has been under the umbrella of the free trade agreement.
Why did the government tell Canadian farmers during the last election that free trade would protect them from U.S. harassment and that they would have open access to the U.S. market when they clearly do not? Were they deliberately misleading Canadians, or are they just too naive to know?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member spent at least a quarter of his time looking at agricultural issues and studying in particular the free trade agreement as it relates to trade of grains between our two countries, he would know that until such time as the subsidy level on the two countries is equal there will be controls maintained.
In this particular case with regard to Durum, the United States is a much higher subsidizer of Durum and wheat products than Canada is. Therefore, we are penetrating that market simply because of the quality and the price. I think that demonstrates clearly the
energy and the enthusiasm that our farmers have displayed in exploiting the U.S. market.

Mr. Speaker, they promised that there would be no harassment. Clearly, there has been.
In the past, Article 11 of GATT has protected our right to have marketing boards and bodies such as the Canadian Wheat Board. By allowing the U.S. to question these programs under the FTA, the government has opened the door to challenges and doubt. In the meantime, Canadian farmers are financially bearing the cost of their actions. How does the government intend to defend our interest to stop this harassment from their buddies to the south?
Will the government vote for Canada and Canadian farmers when the GATT panel decision on ice cream and yoghurt goes before the full GATT body?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, The hon. member cannot have it both ways. He is suggesting that this is a free trade initiative. It is strictly a GATT initiative. I answered that question twice in the House last week to the Hon. Member for Algoma. It has been the subject of a late show in which we outlined very clearly the position of the government. I would invite the hon. member to read those answers.

Mr. Speaker, to continue the speech I had begun before oral question period, I would just like to say that the GST is not a solution, but rather a problem. It does not get rid of the deficit, far from it. Instead, it creates a situation where Canadian business people are in great disagreement with this approach to taxation. Obviously, the burden borne by the middle class will grow. That is also a very important factor. Obviously, all provincial finance ministers disagree with this approach to taxation. All Canadians have shown their disagreement.
Mr. Speaker, a few minutes ago, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) referred to the reason why Canada cannot give more money to the poor countries. He said that the budget would not allow it but if they had inherited a better financial situation, they would have been able to do so. It is rather strange to hear the the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who has been in this House for over 15 years, say such a thing, given that the present Government has been in office for more than five years. How can you explain such a statement knowing that they have been in charge of this country's public affairs for five years, but they are still using that argument that they cannot give more money to the poor countries?

The Canadian people expect an alternative; not alternatives, but rather an alternative. It would be in the best interests of any government in this country to take heed that the Canadian people want their government to reconsider this whole goods and services tax completely.
It has been echoed by many economists in this country that one of our big problems is the fact that the tax system has become so complex that nobody seems to understand whether we are coming or going.
I am sure that an alternative could be looked at. When we see the controversy over the goods and services tax we can go to an alternative. We can be inspired by a document whose principles are still good today, namely, the Carter Commission of 27 years ago. With this document we could make a complete and true reform of the fiscal system in this country. That is an alternative we have to look at and that is going to take a tremendous amount of political will. Unless we have this political will, we are going to lose the confidence of all Cana-

dians, no matter what government is sitting on your right-hand side, Madam Speaker.
In conclusion, obviously this is a subject that could be debated for months on end but, nevertheless, the last opinion should come from Canadians at large. They are not happy with the situation. It is time that the alternative be looked at. It is the only alternative left that can be of any value in bringing back the confidence of the business people and the confidence of Canadians, especially the middle class.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: On questions or comments the Hon. Member for Broadview Greenwood.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to my colleague. My colleague has studied Behind Closed Doors on the Carter Commission and other examples of comprehensive tax reform. In his opinion, why does he not think the Government of Canada, which was so adamant on this change from 1984 to 1988, has not rallied and gone for a comprehensive tax reform, and why has the government just gone for this added bureaucracy of an extra 4,000 to 6,000 public servants on GST? Why do you think the government is not acting in a simpler, fairer and more efficient way?

Madam Speaker, I would say it is very simple. As you mentioned, Behind Closed Doors certainly brought out a lot of facts. The financial elite in this country have been dictating to this government, and to previous governments, in the last 25 years. Under this government with its ideology, I would say the basic problem is that there is no political will nor political courage to look at the matter face to face and say that we need a complete reform because there has been a disproportionate influence from the financial elite in this country.

Madam Speaker, I was very interested in the hon. member's speech, and I was especially interested in the impact because of the importance in his area of the goods and services tax on the tourism industry. I would like to know if the hon. member knows just what the impact will be.
Clearly, the government has made moves already this year which have increased the cost of gasoline and those increases will continue in the next year. In my area I hear a lot of complaints about the amount of taxes which have been added to gasoline in the last four years. This move

now with the goods and services tax will hit eveiy kind of tourism item, such as restaurant meals.
For instance, I recently stopped overnight at a motel in my constituency. The owner pointed out to me that if I returned in 1991 after the goods and services tax is in place to stay overnight, had a cocktail before dinner and then had dinner, the following taxes would be imposed. On the room in Ontario there will be a 5 per cent tax; a cocktail before dinner will have a 10 per cent tax; on dinner there will be an 8 per cent tax. On top of that and on top of all these other taxes plus on the meal itself there will be a 9 per cent federal goods and services tax.
My concern is twofold. Our season for tourism tends to be very short in this country, and so we have a very short period of time in which to make a good living for the small tourist operators.
I want to know from the Hon. Member if he feels that the combination of administrative problems plus the additional goods and services tax will be detrimental to the tourism industry because it is a very important one both in his constituency and in mine.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity- Of course, his question is most appropriate. There was a very interesting article in today's La Presse reporting that the last two years have been disastrous for the tourism industry.
Of course, in the last few weeks I contacted the various tourism organizations in this country, especially the Tourism Industry Association of Canada, and the Conference Board of Canada, which published their reports showing that this tax would indeed be disastrous, especially for the tourism industry.
Despite what the Minister of Tourism is trying to tell us, the facts are there. Everyone else cannot be wrong and they are the only ones who are right! That is impossible! The issue is very simple. This tax will be a nightmare for tourism operators and we will live with it-

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to intervene in this debate to put a perspective, in the brief ten minutes that we have, on my department's involvement in so far as the administration of the GST is concerned. Before I do that I would like to answer the question: Why is the government going ahead with a goods and services tax?
First, let me say that I come from a small business family and I was a small-businessman myself for many years. The answer to the question is very simple. In the good natured rhetoric that takes place in this chamber and outside we sometimes forget why the government is committed to moving ahead instead of staying with the status quo. The easiest thing for any government is to stay with the status quo and not move forward in a progressive and aggressive way for the benefit of future generations and for the benefit of allowing Canadians to reach their full potential.
I think it is a universally accepted fact that the existing federal sales tax is an obstacle in the way for Canadian manufacturers, producers and exporters. I know because I was an exporter, a manufacturer and a producer in Canada. There is nothing more damaging to the potential of the Canadian manufacturer and producer than the existing federal sales tax. I think that is universally an accepted fact. Even our friends the Liberals and New Democrats who agreed on that a year ago are now suddenly asking that this whole GST be dropped.
I cannot understand suddenly the opposition parties coming here for their own political reasons and saying: "No, we cannot go ahead with this, we cannot go ahead with that," without coming forward with any alternatives.
I see one of the Liberal members shaking his head. Obviously, he has not been in the business community because if he had been he would know very well that the existing federal sales tax, while the world changes around us, is a major, obstacle for us to be able to produce and compete on a level playing field with the international market-place and for us to to have free trade.

We are not re-inventing the wheel. There are 48 countries around the world which have a value-added tax. If we do not change, move forward and accept the fact that we have to give our producers an opportunity to compete on a level playing field then we are not going to be able to keep up with the rest of the world and we will fall further and further behind. I do not want that to happen to my children or to anybody else's children in this country without them having full opportunity.
Now what we must do from the standpoint of an administrative situation is make the GST system more workable. It must be understandable and it must impose the least possible addition to the paper burden of both government and the taxpayer and, in particular, the small business community.
To achieve this goal, we have designed a program that emphasizes two key points: consultation and information. In order to facilitate this initiative I have established within the Department of National Revenue a special industry consultation group. The consultation group has begun individual meetings with major national trade and industry associations and professional groups on whom the GST will have a significant and immediate impact. We will be putting special emphasis on sectors that have unique needs, I have already mentioned small business but also charities, financial institutions, farmers and so on.
I can assure all those who accept this open invitation that their views and concerns will be seriously considered because in my view the best way to avoid problems is to consult and we are going to do just that.
I believe by doing that, the consultation process will benefit the government and, more importantly, it will benefit the business community and the taxpayer.
We will also be providing information to those taxpayers who request it. It is for this reason that our information campaign, including registration and information programs which will begin later next year, will be far-reaching. In addition to registration kits and printed information that will be available early in the 1990s, we must provide local seminars and one-on-one assistance to as many registrants as possible. We will do just that. We will provide a service never before witnessed in this country.
Supply
This service, this support, this assistance will need additional resources. I spoke to a group of chartered accountants earlier today. I announced the steps necessary for us to be able to meet this requirement to provide the service, and to be able to meet the needs of an estimated 1.6 million taxpayers as compared to the 75,000 who are currently paying the federal sales tax. By the way, Madam Speaker, that is the reason it is unfair. Why should the tax burden, in this instance of $18.5 billion, fall on the shoulders of 75,000 Canadian producers and manufacturers who will be then hampered in producing more products and creating a better economy and, therefore, establishing greater job opportunities in an international competitive market? So in order to provide this service, we are shooting for a target of between 3,400 and 3,900 additional person-years in order to be able to: (a) administer the goods and services tax; and (b) provide the services that are so necessary particularly to the small business community.
I would like to point out that the ratio compared to the International Monetary Fund is not bad. In fact, it is pretty good. Because I and my officials in this government have spent the last six months or more in looking under every rock, to use that term, to utilize existing facilities, to utilize existing resources, to look forward to innovative methods and ways of dealing with the GST, to find the most state-of-the-art technology possible. That is why our ratio, compared to the IMF, is considerably better. The ratio on the IMF for a value-added tax such as ours is one person for each 250 taxpayers; ours is one person for each 300 plus taxpayers.
So I feel very positive that instead of sitting on the status quo as the opposition parties would want us to do, we are moving ahead. It is very clear that this government is moving ahead with the GST.
The Finance Committee hearings continue. We continue to consult with Canadians, but when we put this measure in place by next year, when we have the one on one involvement with the Canadian taxpayer and the Canadian businessmen, I can assure you that we will be far better off as we move toward the next century. If we had stayed with the status quo, we would not have had a Free Trade Agreement with the United States. If we had stayed with the status quo, we would not be reducing the deficit by $10 million. If we had stayed with the status quo, we would not have created over 1.5 million jobs in this country in the last five years. If we had stayed with

Supply
the status quo we would not have been able to give our children and our grandchildren the opportunity that they deserve.
All of us who are elected to this chamber must put political persuasions aside because if we were doing this only for political reasons we would not be doing it. We are doing this because we believe in Canada and we believe what we are doing is right for the future of Canadians and right for my children and your children. That is why we are not putting any emphasis on a popularity contest.
This is not a simple thing. This is not an easy matter. It is not a popular matter today. But when Canadians see that it is going to give our children the opportunity to reach their full potential I think they will understand that this is the right thing for Canada and for future generations.

Madam Speaker, the hon. minister for the government indicated that this side opposite should have an alternative. Some 80 per cent of Canadians are asking the government to have an alternative, to go back to the drawing board on this proposed tax. Does the government not want to listen? We believe that in the best tradition of parliamentary government when some 80 per cent of Canadians are opposed to this tax, there is a clear message to the government which has the first responsibility to draw up an alternative to what obviously is an obviously wrong tax proposal go back to the drawing board.
I would like to ask the hon. minister some specific questions. Can the minister guarantee Canadians that this proposed tax will not be a powerful and tempting tool to grab taxes from the people?
Second, how can it be workable when even the small businesses say that truly this type of tax is a "gouge and a squeeze tax"? How can you then tell them that this tax is simple when in fact all testimony has told us that it will be confusing, it will be complex as far as record-keeping is concerned, and that there will be many other nightmares in the administration of it?
Third, would not the minister agree that this tax will be a vehicle for greed and dishonesty on the part of government to increase taxes in the future? Last, I submit the minister has to agree that tax even only on
some food, when some people cannot even afford to buy food with their type of meagre earnings, will be a threat to their physical health. A tax on the tools of learning, for those who want to study but can barely afford to study, will threaten their intellectual health. That a tax on death is truly a reflection of insensitivity on the part of government to collect taxes from the dead.

Madam Speaker, I would probably need half an hour to answer in detail all those questions but I will try as quickly as possible to answer the last part of the hon. member's question about basic groceries and low-income Canadians paying tax.
I do not know where he has been for the last three years since this tax proposal began to be debated because it is three years and more specifically since the technical paper came out. But the member will know that basic groceries are exempted. He will know that consultation still continues with the food industry to eliminate any grey areas that exist in that industry. He will know that there is a GST tax credit being offered as early as this December when my department will be mailing out income tax forms to all Canadians for low-income Canadians to be able to register for tax credit. He will know that the low and medium-income Canadians in this country are going to be better off as a result of the GST. He should know as well that by eliminating the obstacles to Canada's manufacturers and producers and opening up greater opportunities for trade and competition all Canadians are going to be better off. So that answers the first part of the question.
Second, will we raise the tax? What a silly question. We have a federal-sales tax, if we wanted to raise taxes, and sometimes you have to raise them, if you are left with a bankrupt economy like the party that he represents left us with five years ago. We cannot continue to put the burden of our deficits on the shoulders of my children and yours. What is the difference whether we raise the GST or whether we raise the existing federal sales tax except for the fact that the Minister of Finance has already stated that the GST is not going to be raised, except under exceptional circumstances, until 1993-94.
Finally, the question that the member asked about grab bag taxes. How can he say that a GST which is a broader based tax is some sort of a grab bag of taxes when we have a $18.5 billion tax grab in the federal sales tax on the shoulders of 75,000 Canadian manufacturers

and producers? That is the unfairness of the existing tax. That is why it is being changed.
We will receive out of the GST some $24 billion, $5.5 billion of which will go back into the economy through tax credits for people earning low and middle incomes. Part of it will go back to assist small business collect the tax. Therefore, the net revenue will wash out in the process while assisting Canada's economy to grow and prosper so that we can all be better off instead of the regressive policies of the Liberals, not to mention the New Democrats. That is why we are doing this, for the betterment of Canada.

Madam Speaker, it is almost a year since the election. During that time, I have risen in this House in numerous debates to explain to the government opposite and to the members about the unfairness of a proposed government program, the harshness of some new policy on the devastating effect of the budget on people who live in the north, on people who live below the poverty line, on aboriginal people, and on women.
The free trade agreement, the deregulation exercise, changes to the post secondary education policy for native people, the Budget, the unemployment insurance changes and now the proposed tax reform. In every instance it is the same story. Those who get hurt the worst are always the women, the poor, the aboriginals, the northerners, Canadians who live in the far extended regions of this country. There are Canadians who cannot pay their mortgages, and most young people cannot afford one.
Students cannot afford the education they need. There are elderly people who cannot afford to pay for their health care and for their rent and food also. People sleep in the streets. The number of homeless is increasing. Farmers are closing down their farms. It is a story as old as history.
The difference between the Conservatives and the Liberals: Tories divide the nation in half, into those temporarily better off and those worse off before and call it recovery; Liberals speak for the minorities and for those who have not yet entered the mainstream, for ethnics who want to add their culture to the mosaic that is Canada, for women who are 52 per cent of the population and 52 per cent of the talent of this country, for young people demanding an education and a future,
Supply
for senior citizens terrorized by the idea that their only security, their social security is being threatened, for millions of reasoning people fighting to preserve our environment from greed and stupidity and fighting to preserve our very existence.
This government has become so arrogant and so elitist that there is no hope for grassroot Canadians to catch up. I read the speech which the Minister of Finance gave recently in New York to the Economic Policy Council of the United Nations Association of the United States. He proudly recited all the "destruction" that this government had caused in our country in the past five years and then said: "We have introduced income tax reform, and are moving ahead to replace our antiquated manufacturers' sales tax with a multi-stage goods and services tax, a value added tax, that will come into effect on January 1, 1991".
The Minister did not even pause, let alone explain to the UN delegation that the entire process is in the hands of Canada's parliamentarians and its citizens. He misled the Canadian public in every ad which he placed in newspapers across the country stating that this tax would be implemented in January, 1991. We as members on this side of the House have become accustomed to these lies and we are no longer surprised at the contradictions and the redundancies. But to lie to his friends in New York, I thought the Minister would be a little more sensitive.
If one of them were to ask how Canadians feel about this tax or how it affects Canadians, would he not have to tell them? I think he would have to tell Americans what they will learn from Canadians: that as a result of the goods and services tax, the gross domestic product will be cut, wage and price increases will spiral, labour costs will increase, as will the Consumer Price Index. There will be employment losses, inflation will rise, interest rates will be pushed up and, contrary to what the finance minister told this UN economic polity group, Canada will have the slowest growth rate in the Group of Seven, which consists of the U.S., Japan, Italy, West Germany, Britain, France and Canada.
This cut in growth will mean a sharp decline in domestic demand which will be reflected by retail sales, housing starts, business investment and government spending. Perhaps government spending will soar when revenue from this alleged revenue neutral tax gets added

October 2, 1989

to the federal coffers. I bet this government gets even bigger when it is handed another cash cow.
I want to mention quickly two more contradictions in the minister's speech which he gave in New York because they illustrate just how redundant this government's policies really are. He talked about the rebirth of belief in market economics.
I was interested in an article in the Toronto Star which expanded on the federal government telling Canadians to put their faith in the market. It said that free trade is good for Canada because it creates one big North American market. The new Progressive Conservative goods and services tax will be a bonanza because it will remove distortions in the market caused by the existing sales tax. For the most part the government's policy is based on a belief that the market makes better economic decisions than a bunch of politicians in Ottawa, but apparently even the Tories do not think that is always the case.
During the last election, for example, the Tories decided they knew more than the market about oil prices and prospects. The market was telling Canadians that energy megaprojects were too risky at the prevailing price of oil. But, since the Tories thought they knew better, they proceeded to commit megabucks to megaprojects. How does that interventionist spirit square with the Tory vision of one big happy market?
Studies have slammed the government for risking billions of taxpayers' dollars on the highly questionable assumption that crude oil prices will rise substantially over the next two decades. If that does not happen, Canada will lose a substantial portion of its megaproject capital. In other words, billions of taxpayers' dollars will go down the drain.
It is too bad the free trade deal does not allow Canada to pass on the Tories' new 9 per cent sales tax to U.S. consumers who may end up buying subsidized Canadian oil.
The third flaw in the minister's speech that day in New York was one we are all akin to: "If we expect to prosper, we shall have to control the destruction of our natural
environment". Is it not ironic that on the eve of shutting down parts of VIA Rail service, the most environmentally friendly means of transportation, the Minister of Finance dares to present to a delegation at the United Nations his government's passionate commitment to environmental protection?
It is like this government's commitment to the poor of this country. The so-called beneficiaries of the tax are to be lower income earners according to the Minister of Finance, but the poor of this country have already lost so much during the reign of this Conservative government through increasing taxes that, on balance, they as well as others have become big losers.
The poorest of Canada's poor are women, for instance. Moving away from a progressive income tax toward a regressive tax on consumption hurts women most because they are in the lower income groups. The credits for those earnings less than 25 per cent are insufficient. It does not compensate for the cost of the sales tax.
For instance, although day care is exempt, the cost of the service could increase because day care operators will pay tax on many items, such as diapers, toys and any other services that they need to carry on their business.
Another group of low-income earners are aboriginal people. I want to mention that credits to low-income earners are not tied to inflation. In reviewing the details of the proposed national sales tax, there does not appear to be provisions to exempt off-reserve treaty Indians from such a tax. Therefore, I do not know whether the government will be implementing a process to reimburse the tax to native people affected. These people have a unique constitutional position on such things as taxation.
Certainly, northerners are not exempt. The proposed tax will cause tremendous problems for consumers and small businesses in the Northwest Territories. It will have a devastating effect on tourism, inflation, transportation and construction costs. Northerners want to develop politically and socially in a way that eliminates uncertainties and encourages northern people to participate fully in achieving self-reliance. We are looking for new avenues to strengthen our economy and to assert our pivotal role in Canada's future.
October 2, 1989

This government is making it almost impossible for the north to develop and for northerners to catch up economically with other Canadians. We have the same right to opportunity as any other Canadian citizen. This government continually implements programs that keep us down.
The budget and this tax reform disproportionately hurts northerners more because we already have the highest cost of living. The dollar value of the tax paid in the NWT will be much higher than the tax on the same item in the south.
Today the minister said the impact of the GST will be minimal on northerners. Yet, after six invitations to the north, this minister has not complied to see for himself. He has not, in fact, tabled the analysis that was done on the GST and the impact it would have on the north.

Madam Speaker, the hon. member listed a number of people who, according to her perspective of society, will need some assistance. I think it is important to draw the distinction that what is important is not that we stare at our feet and look only at those who need assistance, but that we put in place systems that are long term so that a nation and its government have the capacity to give that help. While I do not disagree or debate with the member on some areas where we might be more generous as a nation, I do debate some of the specific examples she gave. She said she knew of a whole host of elderly people who could not get medical service in this country. I dispute that. I do not believe that.
I would not expect her to name them in the House of Commons, but I challenge her to supply the names, because I believe that Canada can be of help. We are helping today and I do not think it is appropriate or fair to suggest otherwise.
She indicated that there is along list of European countries which are doing better than Canada or will be as soon as the GST is through. She should know that when the party she belongs to was last in government, in 1984, Canada's rate of economic growth was in thirteenth place just behind Luxembourg. Today we are second and ahead of every country in Europe.
I would like to ask her what authoritative economic evidence she can put forward. Canada is the only country in the world that has the manufacturing sales tax, the

only country that taxes its manufactured products. We were similar to Argentina which put export assessments on all of its exports, trying to put together a wall around the country. Canada was the only one which tried to export into an external world by taxing against its manufacturing.
Can the member give us one authoritative document that will show that when we make a change to that tax we will lose our competitive edge? Having gone from the position when her party was in government of eleventh in competitive factor to today being fourth in the world, how does she think that this will put us back to where we are behind all the countries in Europe? Can she cite the source that is economically credible, anything at all other than the newspaper articles that she may have read at some time?

Madam Speaker, I would like to say to the hon. member across the floor that I am not the Minister of Finance. If I had the resources of the ministry of finance, I would certainly produce documents to sell the goods and services tax and its merits, which the government is not doing. When this government is willing to give me the statistical analysis it did of the impact of the GST on the Northwest Territories, I will be very happy to try to answer some of your questions. I am not the Minister of Finance. All I can give as evidence is to say if your goods and services tax is so good, then all the Canadian people would be endorsing it. They are not.

Madam Speaker, I want to say a few words on this motion that roundly condemns the government for a variety of issues that would properly fall under the topic of how the government is managing the Canadian economy. I want to say at the outset that I was interested to hear the remarks of the Minister of Revenue a few minutes ago. He said the reason this government was bringing in a 9 per cent sales tax was for the good of Canadians. Over the last several months I have not talked to one Canadian who feels that this 9 per cent sales tax should or could be supported.
That is not quite true. I issued a questionnaire in my constituency. I have begun receiving responses to that

Supply
questionnaire. So far about 2,000 questionnaires have come back opposing the sales tax. Four, perhaps five questionnaires have come back supporting what the government is doing. I do not think this government was either elected on a mandate to introduce such a sales tax or should have the right to proceed with such a sales tax, particularly when you consider the impact that sales tax is going to have on poor and middle income Canadians.
I had an opportunity several weeks ago to be in Nova Scotia, just outside of Sydney on Cape Breton Island. Six out of every 10 individuals in that community are unemployed. The average income in that community is around $24,000 a year. In one of the communities I visited, a mine which employed about 1,300 people is being threatened by closure. This government is not only imposing another 9 per cent levy on disposable income for people who can hardly afford to live now, but on top of that is slashing funding for VIA Rail. VIA Rail very often is the only means of affordable transportation in that region of the country and elsewhere.
Apart from the fact that it is affordable transportation, it is good transportation. I have heard the Minister of Transport make the argument that the government had to cut back on funding for VIA Rail because of heavy government subsidies. There is not a transportation system in this country that could operate without government subsidy, and that applies to the airline industry as well as every other means of transportation in Canada. In fact that is why governments, by public policy, have always supported that kind of transportation.
Years ago Tories believed that transportation held this country together. They also used to believe that the CBC was a vehicle for holding Canada together. I still happen to believe that. These people are hell bent on slashing funding. It is an organization that has proved to be of invaluable service in providing information to Canadians, regardless of whether it be on Vancouver Island or in Newfoundland and Labrador. All you have to do is to go into northern Canada to discover how valuable those institutions are to holding this country together as a nation.
I want to go back to the sales tax because it is so unfair that it is, for me, beyond belief. We are talking about removing another 9 per cent of disposable income from
senior citizens' pockets, from people who are disabled, people who can least afford it.
In Nova Scotia, which I spoke about a few minutes ago, if this sales tax goes through, sales taxes are going to be around 19 per cent. In Ontario, this 9 per cent increase will mean a 17 per cent sales tax.
The Toronto area is supposed to presently be in a very affluent situation. It is not. There are an awful lot of people in Toronto, for example, who are working in part-time jobs, who cannot find full-time work because they do not have the skills. Another area this government is cutting back on is skilled training programs.
Toronto, compared with some other areas of the country, is, generally speaking, better off. However, when you scratch the surface and get underneath, there are an awful lot of people in the Toronto area hurting just as badly as people in other areas of Canada, and this government is not providing solutions. In fact, it has very much been a part of the problem.
I am talking about single-parent families, headed mainly by women, who are having a hard time putting shoes on their kids' feet, clothes on their backs and meals on the table. If this government gets away with this 9 per cent sales tax, it is going to make life even more difficult for those women and their kids. That is one of the reasons why we in the New Democratic Party are going to do everything in our power to prevent this government from doing that to average Canadians.
The Minister of Finance said a number of things prior to the election. He said if they did go ahead and implement this sales tax that it would be visible to consumers, that it would show up on the sales slips at the sales desk. Number two, it would be revenue neutral; that is the government would not be looking to have additional revenues other than what it had prior to eliminating the manufacturers' sales tax, and that it would not go toward decreasing the deficit.
Well, the chairman of the House of Commons finance committee during the election campaign said that the sales tax would prove to be a boondoggle for the government, an increase in revenues. The next day the Minister of Finance was on national television saying that the hon. member for Mississauga South was a loose cannon, he did not know what he was talking about and denied that the government would ever proceed to go into the pockets of Canadians who could not afford it
October 2, 1989

and do that to them. He asked Canadians to trust him. Well, as we all know, they trusted him once again and put this government back into power.
They trusted the Conservatives as well in 1984 when they were first elected. The Prime Minister made the declaration that universality and social programs were a sacred trust. They were not elected two days when they started trying to slash senior citizens' pensions, mothers' allowances, family allowances, and everything else that prior to election day this Prime Minister said was a sacred trust that he was going to protect for average Canadian families. We all know what he did subsequent to that.
In fact, I want to read a quote that I came across this morning. The chairman of that finance committee whom I just spoke about now says that: "the government has killed universality and is dragging the corpse out the back door."
I think the hon. member for Mississauga South is an honest gentleman, and I think he not only calls it the way he sees it, but the way he analyses the evidence that he has before him. I think he is absolutely right on. If this government has not actually killed universality, it is fast on the road to doing it.
I hope the Prime Minister does not make any more promises to Canadians about things being a sacred trust because as soon as he does, you know that sacred trust and that program is going to go right down the tubes.
When that Prime Minister was elected and said "Canada is now open for business", no one in the country thought he meant he was going to sell the whole damned country down the tubes. That is exactly the direction he is heading. Every policy that comes out, whether the government wishes to acknowledge it or not, can be tied to that free trade agreement that these guys negotiated and have not yet concluded.
I think an awful lot of Canadians are beginning to wake up and find that the Prime Minister's assurances once again not only were not to be believed, but were going to be reversed.
Finally, the Minister says that health care is exempt. I met with a group of psychologists two weeks ago who told me that if they provide that kind of service in then-office, it is not exempt from the 9 per cent sales tax. If they do it in a hospital facility, it is exempt. I think at the

very minimum the Minister of Finance should come clean with Canadians and tell us exactly what is exempt, what is not exempt, how it is going to apply it and last, but not least, that he is going to withdraw it in the face of the opposition that there is in the country to that kind of fiscal measure.

Madam Speaker, my friend opposite is more fair minded than many others in the House. I would like him to comment on the fact-this is a basic fact-that Canada is the only industrialized nation in the entire world that puts this special tax on its manufacturers, so that we have 75,000 manufacturers paying over $18 billion in tax.
Would he comment on that in light of the fact that 48 other industrialized nations have moved to this type of tax, often for the very reason that I have just given to him. Do they have more poor people in France, Sweden, Norway and those types of countries for having this tax? That is what he is saying. He is saying that we are going to have more poor people if we do this. I do not think the factual record shows that. Would he please comment.

Madam Speaker, I do not think I said it would make more people poor. I think I said that it would make poor people poorer yet. I think that is a more accurate reflection of what I said.
I think there is general agreement that the thirteen and one half per cent manufacturers' sales tax is unfair and it should be dealt with-

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: How?

How about fairness, for one?
I understand the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs would not understand that word, Madam Speaker, but how about fairness. They ask me again, what would we do. How should we replace it. I say simply with fairness.
Spend more.

But I would argue very strongly against some of the changes that have taken place in the tax system over the last number of years, where this government is more and more clearly being seen as a government of big business. If you shifted some of that tax load back to the corporate sector, from where you have placed it on middle and low-income Canadians,

I think that is how you deal with that unfair thirteen and half percent manufacturers' sales tax.
You do not remove the burden from big business in this country and transfer it over to people who are already being nickeled and dimed to death, to the tune of about $1,800 or more a year in personal income taxes since this group got elected, then come along now and say you are going to ding them for another 9 per cent. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
My friend has said that the poor would be poorer. I do not think the factual record will bear that out either. As he knows, since we have become the government, we have moved to these refundable tax credits rather than deductions. A $4,000 deduction against income helps a very rich person far more than a flat tax credit. That's a good thing and the facts show that people under $30,000 are better off than they would otherwise have been given the fact that more revenues were going to have to be collected. If we had had to collect the revenue under the old system, the poor would be far worse off than with the changes we made.
Under the new program families making less than $30,000 will again get this refundable tax credit which, in principle, I am convinced is the right way to go. How can he say that the poor will be poorer given the fact that they are actually going to get a cheque every few weeks?

Well, Madam Speaker, the logic of that argument is not acceptable to me at all. Rather than deal with that specifically, I would like to remind the member that it is built into the White Paper, as I understood the proposal, that because the tax credit is limited to anything in excess of 3 per cent increase in the cost of living, that tax credit will be reduced eventually until it exists no more, as I understand it. As I understand the White Paper, that is exactly what is set out in the formula. There is no doubt in my mind as well that if this government brings it in, whether they bring it in at 6 per cent and everybody thinks "Oh, my God, thank God it wasn't 9", then within two or three years that thing is going to increase, because it is a cash
cow for governments and that has been the way it is in every other country in the world that has that kind of sales tax. I can see the poor getting even poorer, so I don't accept at all the argument that we will be better off as a result of this measure.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak on this Opposition day, when we have a chance, if one can call it that, to hear the same old cliches.
Those of us who have been here during the past five years will remember that we have had five budgets. After every budget, during the period set aside for Opposition speeches, the Opposition told us that jobs would be lost, that the poor would become even poorer, that Canada was going down the drain, that Canadians wouldn't stand for it and that we would be beaten in the next election.
Madam Speaker, you will of course remember Mr. Wilson's economic statement in November 1984, a statement that identified four major challenges: First, reduce the deficit; second, increase Canada's economic growth; third, promote investment, innovation and competitiveness in business; and finally, help Canadians in need.
These are the four major challenges Minister Wilson identified in 1984. We have made considerable progress since that time, but there is more to do yet. What we still have to do, Madam Speaker, is implement the goods and services tax, Part II of a tax reform that is already under way.
Last year, we introduced a tax credit for the first time, and as you know, Madam Speaker, a tax credit is twice as attractive and twice as profitable as an exemption. And above all, it is the fairest way to treat Canadians, because when you have two Canadians, one who earns $100,000 annually and the other who earns $10,000 annually, under the previous Liberal Government both were entitled to a basic exemption of $3,000. This worked out to a savings of about $300 or $400 for the person who had an annual income of $10,000 but the individual with an annual salary of $100,000 was able to save at least $1,500 on his income tax. This was criticized by the Liberals and the NDP. They said it wasn't fair, while we feel that with a tax credit of $1,000 for everyone, the same amount,
October 2, 1989

whether you earn $10,000 or $100,000, the system is fairer and more equitable.
It is often said that sales tax is regressive. For instance, going back to my first example of a person with an annual income of $10,000 and another person who earns $100,000, when these people have to buy a pair of shoes, for instance, the 9 per cent tax will take a proportionally larger chunk out of the income of the person earning $10,000. And that is why, Madam Speaker, our proposal to change the federal sales tax includes a tax credit, but in this case a refundable tax credit, while today, we have a tax that is hidden, a tax that distorts, that provides for 22,000 exemptions and which at the manufacturing level is as high at 13.5 per cent, a tax nobody sees and nobody knows about. We are removing that tax. We are going to remove it completely and replace it with a 9 per cent tax at the consumer level. Not a ripple effect tax, not 9 per cent at each level and cumulative. It will be 9 per cent from start to finish. Nine per cent is paid once, that's all. And only on new goods, not on used goods! Canadians will see the tax and know why they are paying it.
People on low and middle-incomes, all those people and households with incomes of less than $30,000 per year, will receive a tax credit. They will receive it before the tax comes into force. They will receive the tax credit in December 1990, while the tax becomes effective on January 1, 1991. They will receive the credit on a quarterly basis, so that individuals and families on low-incomes will not be hit by a regressive tax as was the case under the previous Liberal Government, because the 13.5 per cent at the manufacturer's level was paid by everyone, both rich and poor.
Under our system, Madam Speaker, those who can afford to pay will pay, while the others will receive a refund for the amount paid. That is important. That should be emphasized. And that is part of the tax reform that was started last year.
On Saturday, I was in my riding, and I had an opportunity to go to a lunch at the Traverse des ages where about 300 senior citizens are members, and several asked questions before lunch, a lunch where they serve beans which are always very popular, and they said:

So what is this GST? What is this 9 per cent? And when I pointed out to those people that if they make $30,000 or less, they would receive a tax credit four times a year, I can assure you, Madam Speaker, that opinion polls and everything else mattered little to them, because they understood that this tax was for the good of the country and would not penalize them-that is important. That is what makes a tax not regressive: when it applies to those to whom it should apply and is refunded to those who cannot afford it.
Again on Saturday afternoon, Madam Speaker, I was in Pointe-du-Lac to meet with the Mouvement Action-Commerce, the association of Pointe-du-Lac business people, who had an exhibition. Small and medium-sized businesses will be paid by the federal Government to collect our tax, the GST. At the end of the month, if they paid out more in tax than they collected, they will be refunded the difference within 21 days. Madam Speaker, that is what makes a tax right, good for the country, applicable, simple and fair. Small businesses with annual sales of less than $30,000 will not even have to collect that federal tax. The tax is fair, non-regressive broadly based and accompanied with tax credits!
I was listening to the Hon. Member for Beaches- Woodbine (Mr. Young) say just now that they admit the present federal sales tax is not good. They admit that 13.5 per cent is not good. And the Liberal Opposition critics say the same thing. Everyone in this House and on the Standing Committee on Finance agrees that the present tax is not good because it is hidden, it is harmful, etc. But while they agree with that, they do not agree that the alternative tax we are proposing is good, although it meets all the normal criteria that an economist, a tax specialist, a sociologist or a political scientist would wish for a federal sales tax imposed at the consumer level, a tax which has proven itself in 48 other countries. I think that must be emphasized.
More than nine million Canadians earning $30,000 or less will receive cheques from the federal Government before this tax is implemented. You know that nearly 65 per cent of Canadians earn $30,000 or less. So if 65 per cent of Canadians receive a tax credit, it means that the 35 per cent with higher incomes will pay their fair share of the federal sales tax. I think that must be emphasized.

October 2, 1989
Supply
The amount given out will be about $1 per working day for adults and of course somewhat less for children. The new federal sales tax, the GST, was introduced to replace an existing 13.5 per cent tax with a more broadly based 9 per cent tax that is much less regressive. This fits in with what has been done since 1984.
Look at the reduction in public expenditures. In 1984, they were 19.5 per cent of our gross national product. This year, they are 16.5 per cent. Therefore, government spending has gone down in the past five years. We deregulated both the energy and transportation sectors to boost the Canadian economy and help Canadian industries. We privatized Crown corporations which were neither important to nor necessary for Canadians and used to compete directly against the private sector. The Government collected taxes from the people and took that money to offer overly generous grants to companies.
We signed the Free Trade Agreement with the United States and, as you would know, this agreement is bound to help Canadian business. Unemployment declined from 11.2 to 7.8 per cent. A million and a half new jobs have been created in Canada over the past five years. Earlier I heard the Hon. Member for Beaches (Mr. Young) say that unemployment is rampant in Toronto and that people can feel its impact Mr. Speaker, I would suggest the Hon. Member was kidding when he said that. We all know everything is going along just fine in Toronto. Were the riding of Trois-Rivieres experiencing the kind of economic boom they now have in Toronto, I think we would not be complaining. Even at that, we are not that badly off in the riding of Trois-Rivieres.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I see you indicating my time is drawing to a close. The deficit stood at $39 billion when we took office, it is now down to $28 billion. To put it another way, we trimmed the annual deficit down 25 per cent in four years. What does that tell us? That we have had a sound economy. And we have had a sound economy precisely because our policies did encourage investors and Canadian business alike. As I said, the 9 percent GST is part and parcel of the over-all plan.
Seen from that vantage point, Mr. Speaker, I think it is imperative that the legislation to implement this tax be
adopted as soon as possible just so we can be like the 48 other countries which have a fair and acceptable tax system.

Mr. Speaker, I would appreciate the Hon. Member's comments on the following.

This morning, one of his colleagues indicated that he felt that this tax was fair to youths seeking an education in spite of the fact that they will be paying more for then-education. We are talking about 500-plus students from universities, 300-plus students from colleges. He thought it was fair for seniors and people on fixed incomes. Some of them will be hit by this tax in addition to the clawback. He thought that it was fair to small businesses. Small businesses have, almost unanimously to my knowledge, said that the tax will be a nightmare, an absolute disaster. It will be extremely costly. It will make them less competitive.
Canadians generally are going to be subjected to this tax by roughly $600 for the average Canadian family in addition, I might add, to $2,800 in additional taxes during the last five years. I suppose that the member who spoke this morning, and I hope that my hon. colleague here can disagree with him, would suggest that the VIA Rail cuts that will affect 2,900 people if they go as proposed is fair, that the unemployment insurance changes that will affect over .75 million Canadians are fair.
The tourism industry, the food industry, the building industry and many others are opposed to this tax. They recognize that it will increase inflation, that it will shoot up the interest rate, that it will cause a loss of jobs. I would like to have my hon. colleague's reactions to these comments. Please, I beg you not to tell me that the Liberals made us do it.

Try a different approach!

Maybe they are afraid of the truth, but after all, the debt we have today is their fault. And as it happens, the federal sales tax is their fault as well-

October 2, 1989

They didn't have the guts to make any changes.

They should take a course-

speechtext:
You had your chance. It's my turn now.
Mr. Speaker, in 1978, I was studying for a master's degree in tax law, and that was eleven years ago. At the time, we were taught that the federal sales tax system was a disaster for Canada, and that was eleven years ago. Who was in power eleven years ago? Was it Social Credit? No, it was the Liberal Party of Canada which appointed all kinds of commissions but never had the guts to say: This is bad for Canada and we are going to change it. That is what we are doing now. The federal sales tax is bad for Canada, we are going to change it and we are going to have a tax system that is fairer and more equitable for Canadians. And that, Mr. Speaker is what the goods and services tax is all about.
Since the Hon. Member's time has expired, we shall resume debate with the Hon. Member for Hamilton West (Mr. Keyes).

Mr. Speaker, I rise today on the motion proposed by the Leader of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition, which states the total lack of confidence in how the Conservative government is managing our economy.
We are already witnessing the piece-by-piece dismantling of the social safety net. This is a net built with care and concern over decades, yet it is being destroyed in just a period of months. Canadians have long believed in government responsibility to provide systems of health and welfare benefits. We have believed in the right of every citizen to such benefits. We have understood well the Liberal concept that the disadvantaged should be able to free themselves from the excessive burdens of misfortune and should be provided every opportunity to pursue a decent standard of living including a higher education and health care.
What troubles Canadians today and what should concern all of us here in the House is that a new and more dangerous weapon against this right to an afford-
Supply
able, decent way of life, this cannon at the heads of families, is a tax that the government proposes to introduce on virtually every good and service.
The grimiest thing about this proposed tax is that it would amount to a tax on those in our society who are most in need of caring government support. The government boasts that lower and middle-income Canadians would receive tax credits to compensate them. However, the credits would not be indexed to inflation.
Just two weeks ago, I organized a town hall meeting in my riding of Hamilton West to give my constituents the opportunity to present their views and concerns on the GST. Of the 350 people who completely crammed the hall, not one person was in favour of this proposed tax. In fact, my constituents took it upon themselves to present me with over 120 petitions containing the signatures of over 5,000 people, and more are yet to come. The petition calls upon Parliament to reject the proposed goods and services tax.
I invited to this town hall meeting several groups representing various areas of interest in Hamilton. Not only did invited guests make presentations but several other showed up at the last minute to give evidence against this regressive inflationary tax measure. Each group gave presentations which lasted between five and ten minutes, and at the end of all the presentations, I invited questions from the floor.
I might add that the town hall meeting was moderated by Sue Patterson of the chartered accounting firm Peat Marwick Thome. She was there with me at my side. She has over a decade of experience at Revenue Canada in excise taxation. Ms. Patterson provided accurate and unbiased answers to many questions which constituents had regarding the proposed tax.
The groups at the meeting included the Downtown Hamilton Business Improvement Area, the Hamilton Chamber of Commerce, the McMaster University Students Union, the Hamilton and District Funeral Services Association-yes, Mr. Speaker, this tax has you coming and going-Hamilton psychologists had their say, the Hamilton and District Homebuilders' Association, the Hamilton YWCA representing the volunteer sector and the United Senior Citizens of Ontario.

October 2, 1989
Supply
My solemn promise to my constituents and to those in attendance was to carry their message to this government here in the highest court in the land. At the time of the meeting, the Hamilton Chamber of Commerce advised us to watch the newspapers because the Canadian Chamber of Commerce was preparing to announce its position on the tax on the very next day. Well, it did and what people learned was that this large constituency, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, is very concerned about the effects of the tax. In fact, in a press release dated September 21, 1989, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce said that it could not support the government's proposals unless a number of conditions were met. These included the harmonization of the federal-provincial tax base, a common means of collecting the tax by both provincial and federal governments, that the tax be revenue neutral and that it must be visible to consumers.
The Canadian Chamber of Commerce raises some important concerns. It suggests that any new tax must be brought in with co-operation between federal and provincial governments because, as the system is currently proposed, it is estimated that as many as 10,000 individuals would have to be hired to administer the tax.
The Chamber also demands that the tax be visible which the finance minister promised it would be in this very House back in June of 1987. However, the Minister of Finance has left it to the discretion of retailers to either put a sign in their window or a sticker on the till. Last, the Chamber insists that the tax be revenue neutral. Yet, as appears to be the case, the tax will be used to raise revenues for the Government of Canada.
The Minister of Finance proposes to replace an $18.5 billion tax with a $24 billion tax and, according to figures released by the Department of Finance, the GST will take a bigger bite out of poorer Canadians than rich ones. In the case of a couple with a single income of $15,000, the GST will consume 8.1 per cent of that income compared to a couple with an income of $75,000 of which the GST will only consume 4.8 per cent. These are Department of Finance statistics.
On behalf of over 10,000 students, the McMaster University Students Union gave a presentation at our town hall meeting. Students strongly opposed the GST.
Their president, Stephen Longo, summed up the feelings of the students when he said: "It seems strange to us that at a time when education and skilled developed are said to be a priority of this government, that they are promoting a tax initiative that could reduce participation in our post-secondary institutions".
At a recent meeting of the Conservative Party of Canada right here in the capital, the Prime Minister's address underlined this glaring conflict between the GST and access to higher education. The Prime Minister said that higher education was a top priority for his government. He also said that in order to remain internationally competitive, our system must be the best. Hollow words, easily said, but hard to swallow in the face of the GST, because if implemented, the GST will do serious damage to students and education. If Canadians wish to enhance their education by taking upgrading courses, they will be taxed. What will this do to the idea of job retraining for people put out of work due to this regressive tax? Even student service fees will be taxed, increasing the cost of the mandatory fees.
Perhaps most hurt of the students will be the imposition of the GST on student textbooks, which as you know, Madam Speaker, are extremely expensive these days. As Mr. Longo told the meeting, this would mean a tax on the very vehicle of education, the printed page.
Beyond this, the tax will also hurt students because the GST will be placed on restaurant meals, because there is no rebate for student housing, because student transportation and telephone charges will be taxed. This is the government's commitment to education? The students say it expresses a lack of commitment to education.
The government has also made great promises in relation to affordable housing. The Hamilton and District Home Builders Association told our town hall meeting quite a different story. While the Minister of Finance says he will soften the blow somewhat through a proposed rebate system, the Home Builders Association says that housing will become less affordable under the GST. The association says that the new tax would add $3,000 to the cost of a new home, more than six times the cost estimated by the Minister of Finance. The association concedes that the added cost to a new home in Metro Toronto and region under the GST will be over $9,000. The Hamilton and District Home Builders Asso-
October 2, 1989

ciation also said that Canadians should expect their rents to go up significantly under the GST.
Not only will the price of a new home increase, but so too will the cost of renovations. Is the government so naive as to think that while the price of new homes increases, the price of older homes will not increase to keep pace with the market? To quote the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, the tax proposals are: "triumph of greed and politics over reason and sound planning". There you have, Madam Speaker, a message from the constituents of Hamilton West through their elected representative to this government. They say enough is enough.

Madam Speaker, I congratulate the hon. member for his very informative words here today. There was one subject that I kept hearing about back in my riding this past weekend. We had a county fair at which thousands and thousands of people lined up to sign a petition. This is something I think all hon. members would agree is one of their basic rights. A few people came up to me and mentioned the fact that they were not too sure of what this GST would do to disabled people and those less fortunate than us. I am wondering if the hon. member knows exactly what effect this will have on the disabled.

Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Haldimand-Norfolk for his questions. The disabled community in this great country had better brace itself for the onslaught of this proposed GST. It appears that personal attendant care will be taxable, except where the attendant is an employee receiving wages. Now this would not be affected by the GST but if the person is receiving a fee for his service which is, in this particular case, more common, it will be a taxable service.
Another example relates to adapted vehicles, such as vans. Vehicles bought to transport disabled persons are subject to the same 9 per cent tax as those bought to transport others. Now if a lift is bought such as those you see on the side of vans to aid people into the van, they are not charged the 9 per cent tax on that lift. Under the Ontario sales tax, the entire vehicle is exempt, but under this situation, it is not.

speechtext:
Wrong.
