It is not, check the technical paper. Computers fall into a similar category. A disabled person buying a computer would have to pay the extra 9 per cent. Software would be free but the computer is taxed at 9 per cent.
By increasing the cost of computers and vans, this government is placing these items even further out of reach and thereby restricting the participation of disabled people in our society. Although renovations to make a home accessible would not be taxed, there will be a tax on the material used in the renovations. A business that wanted to renovate would be taxed on the contractor's services and this will also, of course, discourage people from making buildings accessible.
I stood here and listened to hon. members across the way speak of concerns. One member said that the Official Opposition was giving us these sony and sad tales. Well, let us have a look at the suggestion of tax credits referred to by government members.
Since the credits and income thresholds are indexed only to increases in the CPI minus 3 per cent, fewer and fewer low-income Canadians will be protected. Let us make for a moment the not-so-unbelievable prediction that inflation is more than 3 per cent annually for each year after 1991. The $24,800 threshold at which families begin to lose the refundable sales tax credit will fall to $21,297 after five years, and to $18,288 after 10 years in constant 1991 dollars. This will mean that within five years, the over half a million low-income Canadians who will be eligible for the full refundable sales tax credit in 1991 will lose either part or all of this credit. After 10 years, over one million low-income Canadians who will be eligible for the full refundable sales tax credit in 1991 will have lost either all or part of this credit.
As more low-income Canadians lose the refundable sales tax credit over time, the value of these credits will also fall since the actual dollar value of the credits is only partially indexed to inflation increases in the CPI minus 3 per cent. Within five years the $275 adult credit will have fallen to $236 in constant 1991 dollars. In 10 years, this $275 credit will be worth $203 in constant 1991 dollars. He cannot produce them fast enough. Gross revenues will soon be measured in the millions of dollars.

There are many other examples of such success stories. There is the Harmon family of Queenstown, New Brunswick and their family-operated custom cabinetmaking business. There is Gilbert Levesque of Grand Falls, New Brunswick and his profitable family-run bakery. There is Kathym Small of White Hills, Newfoundland and her dream to build a ski resort in her home province. All of these examples emphasize the success which ACOA has had in encouraging residents, citizens of Atlantic Canada, to stay at home, to not contemplate the exodus to central Canada which has become the norm and to build their futures and our future.
Atlantic Canada has demonstrated that its entrepreneurs can be world-class when given just half a chance. With people like the Sobbys, the Irvings, the Crosbies, the Cohens, the McCains and the Joudreys, to name a few, we have an example in Atlantic Canada of just what entrepreneurship can become. That is the direction and the thrust of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency which the Leader of the Opposition has criticized so vigorously, so unfairly and so incorrectly.
I will not have time to speak on the goods and services tax to the extent to which I wished, but I would like to say this. It is a balanced and integrated program which will eliminate a regressive and damaging federal sales tax that should have been gone long ago. It will provide a new series of major tax credits to more than nine million families at the lower levels of the earning scale. It will reduce net taxation for every family of income of less than $30,000. It will shift the burden of taxation more fairly to those best able to pay. It will improve indexation benefits for any inflationary impact. Lastly, it will provide special rebates to ensure affordable housing all in one encompassing package.
In due course, when the provinces see fit to recognize the opportunity for creation of a single national sales tax, I predict that Canadians will accept the GST program as one of the most effective alternatives for a progressive consumption tax system so essential to the attainment of our country's financial stability.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party

Madam Speaker, I listened with interest to the comments of our colleague, in particular when he said that this was a good tax because it would provide, as he referred to it, a single national sales tax. I want to know if he is aware of something that some of us are not. Have all the provinces joined in overnight or perhaps
earlier today? If they have done so, I am surprised that the Minister of Finance would have not brought this fact to the attention of the House because it would have been, indeed, an achievement on his part that he would have probably wanted to raise in this House. It would have been interesting to see all the provincial finance ministers all of a sudden agree to this horrible tax. It would surprise us. I ask the member if that has happened as of late, or if it is just a wish of his for the provinces to go along with this grief and suffering tax.
I also want to ask him about something he said. I am paraphrasing here, I do not want to pretend to use his exact words. He said that this tax would make a fairer tax system. I believe he said something to that effect right at the end of his remarks. I want to know if he is aware that the government's own sales tax document which was provided to the committee indicates that a family of four-in other words a family of two adults and two children-with the combined two incomes of $45,000, one person making $27,000 and one person making $18,000, will pay-after this tax is in place $629 more in tax each year as a result of the grief and suffering tax. Is that the Tory definition of fairness?

I am happy that the hon. member has asked me those questions because it permits me to get to a part of my speech that I ran out of time to deliver. First of all, the hon. member did not hear me correctly. I said that when the provinces see fit to recognize the opportunity for creation of a single national sales tax, I predict Canadians will accept the GST program as the most effective alternative for a Progressive Conservative tax system.
The Minister of Finance consulted with the provinces for two years. The onus is on the provinces to join in this tax system. I want to tell you that if you had read in last Thursday's Quorum the article by W.A. Wilson, you would see he predicts that the provinces will have their feet to the fire when the citizens of Canada realize that the reason for two tiers of taxation is because the provinces failed to come to a consensus with the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Finance has no alternative but to proceed with the implementation of the federal financial strategy in this country. I respect him for the courage he has had in doing so. I would certainly express the wish and the hope-I think all of us would-of seeing a single integrated tax system. But the onus is now on the provinces to step up and to come forward with

proposals. I believe we have already had indications from the Minister of Finance that he will listen.
I would like to address the second part of the member's question in which paraphrased me. I will tell you exactly what I said. It was that this tax will shift the burden of taxation more fairly to those best able to pay.
We have talked about how business does not like this tax. We have talked about how the opposition does not like this tax. But there are nine million Canadians who are going to get cheques every quarter under this tax system who are going to like it very much. There are families making less than $30,000 who will have a net benefit from this tax, and they will like it very much. Not enough attention has been given to the benefits that they will receive.
A family of one wage earner with two children making $30,000 will have a net tax saving under this program of $214, contrary to the examples the hon. member so selectively picked.

Madam Speaker, I would like to address my remarks to the first portion of the motion moved by the member for Vancouver Quadra that this House condemns the government for its mismanagement of the Canadian economy, including the threat to impose a new 9 per cent sales tax that is regressive, inequitable, invisible and inflationary.
As someone who has spent much of my working life in educating pupils between the ages of 6 and 19, as well as adults, I want to address the affect of the GST on learning because this proposed 9 per cent tax will be regressive on learning. It will be inequitable on learning,
Supply
it will be invisible, and it will be inflationary on our education process.
There is no other country in the world, the western world especially, that has shown as much disrespect for education and for learning as this country has shown in the last five years. Education is an investment and the students of today are the leaders of tomorrow. This reality is not present in any action this government has taken in the last five years with respect to education. In our era, students realized that higher education meant more secure employment, a more secure future.
It is costing more and more for students to attend a post-secondary institution. According to the Canadian Federation of Students, the average cost per student now is around $10,000. With standard inflation this figure will rise at an incredible rate as this government indulges in its philosophy that only the rich should go to universities and colleges, and the poor should go to work. Otherwise, why would this government, in this new proposed tax, deliberately exclude students from receiving additional refundable tax credits above and beyond the general credit that it is making available to low income singles?
On page 15 of the technical paper we see that starting at the minimum level of $6,175, the additional credit will be paid at the rate of 2 per cent of net income up to the maximum of $140. I understand that finance officials have privately conceded that the minimum was set at $6,000 to specifically exclude students from receiving this additional credit.
Our students will not be eligible for the additional credit even though they will be paying the additional 9 per cent on all their textbooks. They will be paying the additional 9 per cent on their writing paper, their binders, their pens, their pencils, student activity fees, their tutorial fees, their rents, their courses and on their typewriters and word processors.
I understand that some members might wonder if a student can afford a word processor, the student should be able to afford 9 per cent sales tax. There are many gifted and bright students, but because of a learning disability require the assistance of a computer, a word processor, so that they can write their essays neatly and these students who were failing before are now going on to universities. These students, under this proposed 9 per cent sales tax, may not be able to go on to post-secondary education.

Supply
Tories laugh but they have no idea of what is happening in education today.
As legislators we should be aware to some degree of what it is like to be a university student or college student. There is not much time to cook for yourself, just like the MPs, so you tend to eat out. But it is not in fancy restaurants like MPs because you can't afford it. They eat in fast food restaurants.
With the proposed 9 per cent on prepared foods and foods eaten in restaurants students will essentially be paying the 9 per cent tax on most of the food they consume.
Many people would argue that education is a privilege, not a right. The interesting thing about that argument is that is supported mostly by those people who have never had to work too hard for what they have got.
I do not agree with this particular philosophy, I believe very strongly that in this country education is a right. It is a right because people are our most important resource. Anybody who does not realize that should go back to school because they couldn't have learned anything when they were there in the first place. The future of our country depends on how much and how well we educate our young people.
This tax will hit each and every pupil as he or she goes through one of our educational levels, right from junior kindergarten on to university. There will be less money to maintain and improve the learning environment as the various school boards use up more money to administer-and I stress, to administer-the tax when applying for their rebates: rebates for general maintenance services such as cleaning, painting; rebates for desks, chairs, books, pencils, right up to the supply of milk for the younger children.
This government does not realize that there are school boards that must provide breakfast for students before they can be taught. The hon. member for Brampton does not realize that. Maybe in Brampton they do not have to provide breakfast. But in the inner cities of Toronto, the Toronto Board of Education has to provide breakfast for children coming to school. Before they can learn they must have a good breakfast.
There will be less money available to the municipalities to provide day care and community centres as they in
turn apply for their rebates for their own services. From day one, when the child goes to school, his or her parents will have less money to buy books that cost more; less money to buy clothes that cost more; less money to provide tutoring that costs more, but may be necessary; less money to take the kids to the zoo, to the museum, to the art gallery. These things are not a luxury. Educational excursions are not a luxury. Books are not a luxury. In a country where our illiteracy rate exceeds 26 per cent, we cannot afford to make books inaccessible to people in general, let alone our children.
This government has acted in contempt of every single person and every single institution in this country. It has acted in contempt of the seniors citizens of this country. It has acted in contempt of the poor people of this country and less fortunate regions of this country. It has acted in contempt of Parliament on more than one occasion. Now it is acting in contempt of the future of this country, our children and their right to a better life and a better world.
The students of this country are not deceived. They cannot be deceived. What does the Prime Minister think that our students would make out of his statement just a few weeks ago when he said at their national convention that education was a priority in the next four years of his government. What does he think they made of that statement? Does he really have so little respect for the intelligence of the audience? I suppose his direct audience was the Progressive Conservative Party at the time. Does he have so little respect for the intelligence of our students that he thinks they believe him?
He really does think that the people of Canada are going to believe him when he says that we will all be better off with this new tax. However, if he really thinks that, he should make a personal note of all the petitions that are coming in from right across Canada and tabled in this House daily. He should make a personal note of all the protests that are being organized across this country.
The Prime Minister does not have any choice if he wants to win the next election. Although his credibility is shot, he had better scrap the tax and go back to the drawing board. There should be no discussion in this House or outside this chamber whether to include all foods, whether to reduce the 9 per cent to 6 per cent. The bottom line is that the GST must be scrapped.

I am interested in a couple of points raised in the hon. member's comments.
First, he talked about the students of today being the leaders of tomorrow. I hope the hon. member also realizes that the students of today are the taxpayers of tomorrow who will have to deal with the issue of deferred taxation which is mounting daily. I wonder how the member proposes to give us constructive alternatives to the GST and the government's tax reforms.
Second, I wonder if the hon. member recognizes that the government proposes to bring in a system of tax credits which will, of course, help students. Do you have any evidence that students will be excluded from the $140 single person tax credit? Do you have any evidence of that? If so, could you table it for us.

It is very clear that the member did not listen to a word that I said. He asked whether the students of today will be the taxpayers of tomorrow. Yes, they will be. That is why we have to provide the best education possible to these students, so that they will be in higher income brackets and will be able to afford to pay the taxes. If we do not have that, we will have a tax revolt in this country and no one will want to pay taxes.
May I quote to the hon. member from his minister's document, the technical paper, on page 89. This is how the government hides things. They talk about what is being exempt, and then they say that hence, as a general rule instruction and training in sports, recreational or cultural activities such as dancing, skating, cooking, sailing or swimming will be taxable.
Private ballet lessons, is this not an investment in our country? Could this not lead to a very profitable vocation for that person? That person will be taxed and may have to drop private ballet lessons. Students may have to drop private music lessons. Yet that could be their vocation. It could be their occupation.
What about the students who will not be able to go on to university because of the 9 per cent tax? Whereas if they finish university, they could be in the hon. member's category earning $60,000 or more instead of earning $20,000 and not being able to afford this tax. I am glad the hon. member posed this question. Let us educate our

young people so that they can afford to pay those terrible taxes put on by this Tory party.

Madam Speaker, I listened with interest to the hon. member's excellent speech and I am sorry that the hon. member who asked the last question did not. He might have understood the problem. I wonder whether I could ask my hon. friend from Parkdale-High Park a question concerning the fairness of the imposition of this tax.
The government has said that this is all necessary and that it is part of their budget cutting process. This is stage two of tax reform. Stage one was introduced before the election. That was lowering the income tax. The details of this tax have only just been released.
In his area of Toronto, is it his view that if the details of this tax had been released before the election that the present government would have been elected, or is it safe to assume that if these details had been made public some time before November, 1988, we would have seen the defeat of the present government? In fact, we might not be enduring these taxes at this time.

I think the answer is self-evident. If the Conservative party was honest during the election they would be sitting on this side and not where they are today. They deceived the public, and it is all coming out now, on VIA Rail cuts, on promising not to increase taxes and now on the 9 per cent. They deceived the public on universality. They will not touch pensions and so on. Now they are clawing everything back.
Here is a party that got in by default and by deceit. They will not be there long. Come 1992 they will be on this side of the House.

Madam Speaker, I could not sit here all day without getting into the debate because I have sat and listened to the opposition ad nauseam today. Although I was not here last Thursday, I read the record from Hansard.
It is very obvious that what this government has to do first and foremost is to take the opposition on a training program so that they can understand how the goods and services tax works and how it will benefit this country. The examples that were given this afternoon by the members opposite were totally false.

October 2, 1989
Supply
I find it rather amusing that the Leader of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition, the man who goes around this country bragging that he was the last one to have a balanced budget in this country was also the individual who raised government spending some 27 per cent in one year and started deficit financing. He does not talk about that. Yet, he comes in here and has the nerve to bring in a motion that states:
That this House condemns the Government for its mismanagement
of the Canadian economy,-
History has shown that he was probably one of the worst managers of the economy in this country. That is absolutely true. We today in this country can thank him because he fathered deficit financing. He fathered the deficit that we are experiencing today and the Liberals thought that was pretty good, and we keep on borrowing, and keep on borrowing, and keep on spending and adding to the debt by some 24 per cent a year.
We have a tax system in this country that needed revision and a man with foresight and with guts, our finance minister, in November 1984 made it very clear to the Canadian public that this government was going to grab this terrible tax system that had been established over the years and reform it to the betterment of this country. He has done just that. I will put his record in finance up against any finance minister this country has ever had, especially the Chretien, Lalonde, MacEachen and Tbmer that we have had over the last number of years. I will put his record against any of them any day.
This new tax is replacing a very outdated manufacturers' sales tax, absolutely outdated, and all three parties agree on that. All three parties unanimously have said in the House that it has got to go, that it penalizes the economy of this country, absolutely. It has been stated in the House by the finance Committee. There is no question about that.
The Liberals flirted with it back in the early 1960s. Back in the 1950s they even suggested perhaps they should do something about this tax. But this is the first government that has had the guts to tackle this major problem that Canadians have with the manufacturers' sales tax. This could destroy our exporting, and we are an exporting nation. We export 35 per cent approximately of what we produce.
If we cannot maintain competition with the nations that buy our goods and services, then we will be out of the market-place. Number one, the manufacturers' sales tax places us at a great disadvantage in exports. Number two, the goods and services tax makes imports less expensive than a comparable product made here in Canada. That puts our producers very much at a disadvantage because they are taxed entirely differently. Third, we are the only country in the world that has a manufacturers' sales tax.
We are late in doing this. This should have been done years ago. Forty-eight other countries have a goods and services tax, the countries that we compete with, and their businesses and their services have no input tax costs and sales tax. Ours do.
The examples that were given today by the members about trying to compare the manufacturers' sales tax with a goods and services tax I must say were totally wrong, totally misleading-I will not say deliberately so because I just do not think they understand. I just do not think they understand.
The goods and services tax is going to make our economy more competitive, both in our export markets and at home. That is very important. Any economist looking at this will tell you that it means jobs. There is no question about an increase in jobs, an increase in productivity in this country, and it is going to help the gross national product of Canada. There is no question about that.
Look at the groups that are appearing before the committee. None of them are arguing that there should not be a GST. They are not arguing there should not be a GST. Well, some of them want it a little lower. Some of them want exemptions. They want to be exempted. They think that they should be exempted but everything else is fine. They think we should have a lower rate, but that is impossible. This government is on the right track. It is going to be implemented in 1991 and by 1992 the Canadian public will understand how good this is for Canada and this government will be re-elected for decades to come.
